pool.q: What is the etiology of primary congenital glaucoma in most patients?
pool.rationale: Primary congenital glaucoma usually occurs sporadically, but it can rarely be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Specific genetic mutations have been identified in some patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What constitutes the classic clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma?

options.b: photophobia, corneal edema, and corneal enlargement
options.c: corneal edema, Haab striae, and buphthalmos

pool.rationale:
Epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm constitute the classical clinical triad of primary congenital glaucoma. Other signs include clouding and enlargement of the cornea (first figure). Photophobia, epiphora, and blepharospasm result from the glare and epithelial abnormalities associated with corneal edema and opacification. Corneal edema results from elevated IOP and may be gradual or sudden in onset. Corneal edema is often the presenting sign in infants younger than 3 months. Microcystic edema initially involves the corneal epithelium but later extends to the stroma, often accompanied by one or more curvilinear breaks in Descemet membrane (Haab striae, second figure).
Although the corneal edema may resolve with IOP reduction, a scar will remain permanently at the site of the Haab striae. A number of other conditions may also cause corneal edema or Descemet tears (such as birth trauma). Corneal enlargement occurs with gradual stretching of the cornea as a result of elevated IOP. A corneal diameter of greater than 11.5 mm is suggestive of glaucoma in a newborn, while a diameter greater than 12.5 mm suggests glaucoma at the age of 1 year. Glaucoma should be suspected in any child with a corneal diameter greater than 13.0 mm. Blepharophimosis is not a clinical feature of primary congenital glaucoma.


(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred first-line treatment for primary congenital glaucoma in a child with an edematous cornea?
pool.rationale: The primary treatment for childhood glaucoma is surgery. The first-line treatment for primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is angle surgery, either goniotomy or trabeculotomy. Because goniotomy requires an incision to be made across the trabecular meshwork under direct gonioscopic visualization, a clear cornea is necessary to enable this surgery. In a child with PCG and an edematous cornea, trabeculotomy would be the preferred treatment. In trabeculotomy, an external approach is used to identify and cannulate the Schlemm canal and connect it with the anterior chamber through incision of the trabecular meshwork. A tube shunt or cyclophotocoagulation can be used to treat PCG but are used only if angle surgeries have failed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following surgery for congenital cataract, what finding predisposes a child to glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Aphakic glaucoma is a common form of secondary glaucoma in childhood. It often develops years after cataract surgery, but it can occur within weeks to months of surgery and is a lifelong risk. Those who have cataract surgery during infancy are at highest risk for glaucoma development, and the risk appears to be even higher in patients with microcornea or persistent fetal vasculature.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 2-day-old infant has tearing and photophobia. Examination under anesthesia reveals horizontal breaks in Descemet membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Pertinent clinical features in congenital glaucoma include (1) corneal edema; (2) increased corneal diameter (greater than 12 mm); (3) elevated intraocular pressure; (4) Haab striae, which are tears in Descemet membrane oriented horizontally or concentric to the limbus.
Birth trauma, on the other hand, presents with corneal edema but with vertical or oblique posterior corneal striae. Peters anomaly presents with a central congenital corneal leukoma, iris strands adherent to leukoma, and variable involvement of the crystalline lens. Sclerocornea presents with noninflammatory scleralization of the cornea with an ill-defined limbus, and vascularization that can affect part of the cornea or the entire cornea. It is commonly associated with cornea plana and angle structure malformation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When no other family history of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) exists, what is the chance that a parent with PCG will have a child with PCG?
pool.rationale: PCG usually occurs sporadically but can be inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. Four chromosomal loci (GLC3A, GLC3B, GLC3C, GLC3D) have been identified, and 2 genes, LTBP2 and CYP1B1, have been shown to cause PCG. The chance that an affected parent will have an affected child is 2%.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 6-week-old boy presents with unilateral epiphora, blepharospasm, and photophobia. The cornea is enlarged but clear. The intraocular pressure (IOP) is 38 mm Hg. What is the preferred initial treatment?
pool.rationale: The classic triad of congenital glaucoma is epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm. The initial treatment is surgical, with goniotomy or trabeculotomy preferred for the initial treatment. Primary trabeculectomy has a high failure rate and is contraindicated as primary treatment. Both Ahmed valve placement and cycloablation are reserved for secondary treatments.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common inheritance pattern in inherited cases of congenital glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Primary congenital glaucoma, also commonly called congenital or infantile glaucoma, usually occurs sporadically, but it can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. One gene, CYP1B1, on band 2p21, has been shown to cause primary congenital glaucoma.
Juvenile-onset glaucoma and the anterior segment dysgenesis syndromes are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy has mitochondrial inheritance.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most likely cause of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) in a 18-month-old boy?

options.b: anteriorly rotated iris stump causing angle closure
options.c: pupillary block due to small, globular lens

pool.rationale:
Primary congenital glaucoma is characterized by isolated trabeculodysgenesis, which accounts for the majority of primary pediatric glaucomas. Most cases are diagnosed within the first year of life, and prognosis is best when glaucoma is diagnosed between 3 and 12 months of age.
Glaucoma associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome may occur in infancy or late childhood with the former being more likely. When glaucoma develops in infancy in this syndrome, the mechanism is isolated trabeculodysgenesis, whereas in late childhood or adolescence, the mechanism is elevated episcleral venous pressure due to the arteriovenous shunts in episcleral hemangiomas.
Pupillary block due to a microspherophakic lens is seen in Weill-Marchesani syndrome and usually presents in late childhood or young adulthood. High myopia with a shallow anterior chamber in a young adult should raise suspicion for this condition.
Aniridia is characterized by profound iris hypoplasia, which is present at birth. Glaucoma, however, may develop in late childhood or early adulthood, possibly due to postsurgical changes in patients who have had angle surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What abnormally developed ocular structure is the pathologic cause of primary congenital glaucoma?
pool.rationale: The basic pathophysiologic defect in primary congenital glaucoma is decreased aqueous outflow due to abnormal development of neural crest–derived tissue of the anterior chamber angle. Although abnormalities of the Descemet membrane, iris, and optic nerve all occur in primary congenital glaucoma, they are secondary effects from the increased intraocular pressure that occurs in this disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the inheritance pattern of juvenile open-angle glaucoma (JOAG)?
pool.rationale: Juvenile open-angle glaucoma (JOAG) is associated with the GLC1A myocilin gene (MYOC). It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is usually inherited as an autosomal recessive trait and associated with numerous genes, including GLC3A, GLC3B, GLC3D, LTBP2, and CYP1B1. Childhood glaucoma is not typically inherited as an X-linked recessive disease or as a mitochondrial disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular condition are curvilinear tears in Descemet membrane most often seen in?
pool.rationale: Tears in Descemet membrane (Haab striae) are seen because of a rapid stretching of the cornea in primary congenital glaucoma. They are not seen in congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) or Peters anomaly. Trauma from amniocentesis can result in a penetrating injury of the cornea. Tears in Descemet membrane can also be seen in a forceps injury sustained during delivery, but these are usually linear, not curvilinear.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 3-year-old child has a history of primary infantile glaucoma. The child's condition remains poorly controlled despite maximal medical therapy and previous goniotomy on 2 separate occasions. What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
pool.rationale: Surgical intervention is the treatment of choice for primary congenital glaucoma presenting in infancy and early childhood. Angle surgery (ie, goniotomy or trabeculotomy) is the preferred initial surgical intervention. Usually, a second angle surgery is attempted before proceeding to alternative surgical interventions. If this fails, then the best next procedure is the placement of a glaucoma drainage device implant with a Molteno, Baerveldt, or Ahmed device.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What are the gonioscopic findings in a patient with plateau iris configuration?

options.a: an open angle that narrows upon indentation
options.b: a narrow angle that opens easily upon indentation
options.c: a narrow angle that reveals synechiae upon indentation
options.d: a narrow angle with a peripheral iris hump upon indentation

pool.rationale:
Plateau iris configuration is caused by anterior rotated ciliary processes that hold up the peripheral iris. The anterior chamber is narrow peripherally but deep centrally, with a flat iris approach. On indentation, a peripheral hump is seen where the iris is draped over the anteriorly placed ciliary processes.
In a narrow angle caused by pupillary block, indentation would either open the angle or reveal peripheral synechiae.
An open angle can narrow on indentation if a large diameter Goldmann lens is used for gonioscopy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the desired observed treatment effect during endocyclophotocoagulation (ECP)?
pool.rationale: Endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation is performed through a clear corneal or limbal incision with direct visualization of the ciliary processes. Power is titrated to achieve shrinking and whitening of the ciliary processes. Bubble formation and ciliary process rupture should be avoided to minimize postoperative inflammation. Photocoagulation lightens rather than darkens the tissue.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What corneal complication is most likely with the use of antifibrotic agents for trabeculectomy?
pool.rationale: Antifibrotic agents, especially 5-fluorouracil, are toxic to the corneal epithelium and can cause persistent corneal epithelial defects. Endothelial damage can occur with the use of antifibrotics but is not common with the current surgical technique and dosage. Keratic precipitates and band keratopathy are not associated with the use of antifibrotic agents.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an advantage of fixed-combination medical therapy for glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Advantages of combination medical therapy include decreased preservative load and improved patient adherence.
Combination drugs containing brimonidine use the highest concentration of 0.2%, which has a higher incidence of adverse events than the lower concentrations of 0.15% and 0.1%.
Timolol 0.5% is the commonly used concentration in combination and monotherapy. Timolol 0.25% is also available as monotherapy but is not commonly used; this concentration is not available in combination products.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition is associated with elevated episcleral venous pressure?
pool.rationale:
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) is a chronic systemic disorder involving vasculitis of small- and medium-size vessels in many organs but most commonly of the upper respiratory tract and the kidneys. There is no known association with elevated episcleral venous pressure (EVP).
Angle recession occurs when the ciliary body is torn, usually between the longitudinal and circular fibers. The typical gonioscopic appearance consists of torn iris processes, visible scleral spur, and an abnormally widened ciliary body. Though there may acutely be microhyphema, there is no EVP or reflux of blood into Schlemm canal.
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is characterized by a prominent anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line, iris hypoplasia, corectopia, and dental anomalies. There is no association with EVP.
Elevated episcleral venous pressure (EVP) can be caused by venous obstruction (as in thyroid ophthalmopathy or retrobulbar tumor) or arteriovenous anomalies (as in carotid-cavernous sinus fistula or Sturge-Weber syndrome).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of glaucoma medication has been associated with an increased risk of post-cataract surgery cystoid macular edema (CME)?
pool.rationale:
Prostaglandin analogue use has been associated with CME, especially in high-risk eyes (ie, aphakic eyes, pseudophakic eyes with open posterior capsules, and eyes with uveitis).
The use of beta blockers, alpha agonists, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors is not associated with CME.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How is uveoscleral outflow affected by age, pressure, and cycloplegia?

options.a: pressure-insensitive, increases with age, increased by cycloplegic agents
options.b: pressure-sensitive, increases with age, decreased by cycloplegic agents
options.c: pressure-insensitive, decreases with age, increased by cycloplegic agents
options.d: pressure-sensitive, decreases with age, decreased by cycloplegic agents

pool.rationale: Uveoscleral outflow is the nontrabecular outflow of the eye. It is pressure-insensitive and the predominant mechanism is one of aqueous passage from the anterior chamber into the ciliary muscle and then to the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces, exiting the eye through an intact sclera or along the nerves and the vessels that penetrate it. It can account for up to 45% of the total aqueous outflow. Uveoscleral outflow decreases with age and in patients with glaucoma. It is increased by prostaglandin analogues, and cycloplegic and adrenergic agents and cyclodialysis clefts early on. The opposite effect is seen with miotics. Outflow for the uveoscleral pathway cannot be measured and is therefore calculated by the Goldmann equation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with controlled glaucoma requires cataract surgery. Intraoperatively, the pupil dilates poorly and the lens tilts with minimal manipulation. What slit-lamp finding might be expected?
pool.rationale:
Poor pupillary dilation and zonular weakness are common findings in pseudoexfoliation syndrome. In addition to exfoliative material on the pupillary margin and lens surface, peripupillary transillumination defects are common. Endothelial pigment deposits, narrow angles, and a more heavily pigmented trabecular meshwork are other related findings.
Corectopia (Rieger anomaly, Axenfeld anomaly, trauma), posterior embryotoxon (anterior segment dysgenesis), and back bowing of the iris (pigment dispersion glaucoma) are not features of pseudoexfoliation or pseudoexfoliation glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what gene are mutations associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome?
pool.rationale:
LOXL1

Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is associated with LOXL1 mutations at 15q24. CYP1B1 is associated with primary congenital glaucoma; FOXC1, with iridogoniodysgenesis; and PITX2, with Rieger syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What pattern of visual field defect is most typical of glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Patterns of visual field loss in glaucoma correspond to the retinal nerve fiber layer anatomy. Glaucomatous visual field defects include arcuate scotoma, paracentral scotoma, nasal step, altitudinal defect, temporal wedge, and generalized depression. An arcuate scotoma is an arc-shaped defect that occurs 10 to 20 degrees from fixation; a complete arcuate defect arches from the blind spot to the nasal raphe and is wider and closer to fixation on the nasal side. This defect is a result of nerve fiber bundle damage at the superotemporal or inferotemporal disc, common areas of damage in glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
A centrocecal scotoma involves both the blind spot and the point of fixation and is seen in conditions such as toxic optic neuropathy, nutritional optic neuropathy, and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Hemianopic defects are caused by retrochiasmal disease, and blind spot enlargement is more often seen in papilledema and chorioretinal inflammatory conditions such as multiple evanescent white dot syndrome and acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide?
pool.rationale: As the leading cause of irreversible blindness in the world, glaucoma poses a significant public health problem. It has been estimated that by 2020, approximately 80 million people worldwide will have glaucoma, with 11.2 million bilaterally blind as a result
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What instrument is most accurate when measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in the setting of corneal scarring?
pool.rationale: In the setting of corneal scarring, devices that can applanate a small area of unaffected cornea, such as the Tono-Pen or pneumotonometer, are more accurate. Although the Goldmann tonometer is considered the standard for IOP measurement, its accuracy and reliability are reduced in the setting of corneal edema and corneal scarring. The Perkins tonometer is a portable version of the Goldmann instrument and has the same limitations. A noncontact tonometer uses an air puff to distort the cornea. The reflection from the air puff may be asymmetrical and distorted in the setting of corneal scarring, resulting in variations in readings for different areas of the cornea.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What mechanism of angle-closure glaucoma is effectively treated with an iridotomy?
pool.rationale: An iridotomy specifically addresses pupillary block. It allows equalization of the pressure between the anterior and posterior chambers in cases where aqueous cannot easily flow through the pupil. This, in turn, relieves any iris bombé that can lead to angle closure. An iridotomy is not useful in cases of synechial angle closure, including neovascular glaucoma and iridocorneal endothelial syndrome. It also does not relieve any posterior pushing mechanisms of angle closure, such as aqueous misdirection, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, or anterior choroidal effusions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with angle-closure glaucoma (ACG). What patient characteristic should prompt the surgeon to consider plateau iris in the differential?
pool.rationale: Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) is caused by pupillary block. Risk factors include older age, female gender, race (Alaskan Inuits and Asians have highest prevalence), family history, and hyperopia. Most patients with PACG have hyperopia, with bilateral narrow angles. Myopia and younger age should prompt the surgeon to consider plateau iris as the underlying cause, as high myopia and angle closure may be due to microspherophakia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a unique hazard with cataract surgery in eyes with nanophthalmos?
pool.rationale: All of the listed complications (nonrhegmatogenous retinal detachment, suprachoroidal hemorrhage, aqueous misdirection) may occur with intraocular surgery in a nanophthalmic eye, but intraoperative or postoperative uveal effusions are unique occurrences in the setting of nanophthalmos. Some surgeons advocate prophylactic scleral windows inferiorly to manage intraoperative and postoperative uveal effusions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old patient with neovascular glaucoma presents with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 56 mm Hg on maximal medical therapy. The iris neovascularization is starting to regress after anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment several days prior and vision is 20/30. What is the best treatment for this patient?
pool.rationale: Neovascular glaucoma causes uncontrolled IOP due to secondary angle closure from a fibrovascular membrane. This prevents all angle procedures, including laser trabeculoplasty, iStent, Trabectome, and canaloplasty. In general, trabeculectomy has a low success rate in these cases, particularly when the eye is still inflamed. Cyclodestructive procedures can be useful, but they are generally avoided in patients with good vision who are reasonable surgical candidates. A primary tube shunt is the best option in this case.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with bilateral narrow angles and acute angle-closure glaucoma in the left eye. What is the next step in treatment for the right eye?
pool.rationale:
Laser peripheral iridotomy is the next step in therapy for a contralateral eye at risk for angle-closure glaucoma.
Primary angle closure (PAC) is a bilateral disease. Patients are at high risk of developing acute angle closure in a fellow eye that shares the same anatomical predisposition for increased pupillary block, especially if the inciting factor includes a systemic sympathomimetic agent (nasal decongestant or anticholinergic agents) or emotional stress response.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What treatment may reverse elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) prior to filtration surgery for neovascular glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Panretinal photocoagulation has been shown to reverse IOP elevation in early angle-closure neovascular glaucoma (NVG) where synechial closure has not exceeded 270 degrees. Anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy may also be useful in this setting, although it is not offered as a choice in this question. Topical IOP-lowering medications, including alpha agonists, are used in NVG. Topical corticosteroids are used to help with pain and inflammation but do not lower IOP. Strict glucose control is discussed with all patients for systemic control of diabetes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What initial therapy should be avoided in a 35-year-old patient with moderate glaucoma and a history of asthma?
pool.rationale: Prostaglandin analogs and topical beta blockers are often used as initial therapy in glaucoma patients because they can achieve a 20% to 30% intraocular pressure (IOP) reduction with once-daily dosing. In this patient, a prostaglandin analog, alpha-agonist, or carbonic anhydrase inhibitor would all be options, likely favoring the once-a-day dosing of a prostaglandin.   Nonselective beta blockers (such as timolol) should be avoided in patients with reactive airway disease, as they can cause bronchospasm. Nonselective beta blockers should also be used with caution in patients with hypotension, bradycardia, and heart block. Selective beta blockers such as betaxolol are safer to use in patients with asthma than nonselective beta blockers; however, they are also less effective than nonselective beta blockers.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What factor will cause a falsely low intraocular pressure by applanation tonometry?

options.a: thicker than average central corneal thickness

pool.rationale: The accuracy of applanation tonometry is affected by a variety of factors. A falsely low IOP is associated with thinner than average central corneal thickness, inadequate fluorescein with thin mires, corneal edema, and certain gases used for induction of anesthesia. A falsely high IOP is associated with thicker than average central corneal thickness, excessive fluorescein with thick mires, applanating over a corneal scar, Valsalva maneuver, eyelid squeezing, and pressure on the globe.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most reliable way to assess a narrow angle?
pool.rationale: Gonioscopy continues to be the gold standard of angle evaluation and provides more information than current imaging techniques. While ultrasound biomicroscopy and anterior segment OCT can provide valuable information, the particular advantage of gonioscopy lies in the ability to indent, allowing one to assess whether peripheral anterior synechiae have formed in the setting of a narrow angle. This is particularly important because the management of appositional versus synechial angle closure is different; a peripheral iridotomy is not indicated if the angle is synechially closed 360°. The van Herick method is a quick way of assessing angle depth, but does not give any direct information about angle anatomy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: By what mechanism do topical beta blockers reduce intraocular pressure?

options.d: reducing aqueous production by the ciliary body epithelium

pool.rationale:
Topical medications for the treatment of glaucoma can reduce the formation of aqueous and/or improve outflow of aqueous. Topical beta blockers reduce aqueous production by the ciliary epithelium by inhibiting cAMP production. This reduces aqueous secretion by 20% to 50%. Alpha agonists also reduce cAMP production via binding to the alpha 2 adrenoceptors.
With long-term use, brimonidine has been shown to also increase uveoscleral outflow. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors inhibit ciliary epithelium carbonic anhydrase, which reduces aqueous production. Parasympathomimetics cause contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle fibers, which in turn increases outflow through the trabecular meshwork by causing tension on the scleral spur. Prostaglandin analogues increase uveoscleral outflow through an unknown mechanism, though it is thought to be through activation of matrix metalloproteinases, which in turn remodels the tissues along the uveoscleral pathway.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old Asian female comes for a routine eye exam except she feels as though her vision has been slowly worsening over the past year. A complete ocular examination is performed.  The anterior segment examination is unremarkable except for trace nuclear sclerosis in both eyes and an intraocular pressure measurement of 28 mm Hg OU. Gonioscopy reveals bilateral, relatively symmetric scattered peripheral anterior synechiae. The patient's ocular history is unremarkable. What is the most likely cause of this patient's gonioscopic findings?
pool.rationale: Chronic angle-closure glaucoma (CACG), also known as creeping angle closure, is largely asymptomatic and is therefore often diagnosed in later stages, similar to primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). It is a major cause of blindness in Asia. If gonioscopy is not performed, the diagnosis of CACG may be missed and the patient incorrectly labeled as having POAG.  Treatment may involve laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) to prevent progressive peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) development; however, the angle can continue to develop PAS even with a patent LPI, and patients need serial gonioscopic examinations. Topical ocular hypotensive medications may be used in conjunction as well. Eventually, filtering surgery may be necessary.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the main disadvantage of using indirect ophthalmoscopy for optic nerve examination?

options.d: requires use of a contact lens

pool.rationale: Indirect ophthalmoscopy does not require as much patient cooperation as a slit-lamp fundus examination and is performed with the aid of a noncontact condensing lens. It is therefore useful in examining young children and uncooperative patients. However, it does not provide adequate magnification to assess subtle features of the optic nerve and tends to underestimate cupping.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 80-year-old man with open-angle glaucoma (OAG) complains of fatigue. What glaucoma medication is most likely to cause this side effect?
pool.rationale:
Systemic side effects of brimonidine include fatigue and dry mouth.
Although loss of energy is commonly associated with the use of oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs), the topical CAIs (dorzolamide and brinzolamide) rarely cause systemic side effects.
Fatigue is not associated with the use of pilocarpine or latanoprost. Flu-like symptoms, along with muscle/joint pain and headaches, have been reported with latanoprost. Systemic adverse effects from parasympathomimetic agents have been seen mainly with the use of indirect-acting agents (eg, echothiophate) and include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and increased salivation. Pilocarpine, a direct-acting parasympathomimetic, typically does not cause systemic side effects.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient reports evolving right visual field loss in the setting of new photopsias and floaters. Intraocular pressures of the right and left eyes are 34 mm Hg and 15 mm Hg, respectively. If performed, aqueous aspiration would likely demonstrate a higher concentration of what substance in the sample from the right eye?
pool.rationale:
This clinical vignette alludes to case of a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment with associated intraocular pressure elevation, which is known as Schwartz-Matsuo syndrome. While rhegmatogenous retinal detachments typically lower intraocular pressure, occasionally they can be associated with elevated intraocular pressure. When this occurs, it is thought to be caused by migration of liberated photoreceptor outer segments into the anterior chamber angle, where they obstruct aqueous humor outflow in the trabecular meshwork.
Red blood cells and lens protein are possible causes of trabecular meshwork obstruction in hemolytic and phacolytic glaucoma, respectively. CMV is thought to be the causative etiology in the trabeculitis of glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For what type of glaucoma is indentation (dynamic) gonioscopy most helpful in determining a treatment plan?
pool.rationale:
Indentation gonioscopy is used to determine appositional versus synechial angle closure. In primary angle-closure glaucoma, the extent of synechial angle closure determines whether or not iridotomy should be performed. In the absence of significant peripheral anterior synechiae, iridotomy should be performed even if the intraocular pressure is well controlled with medical therapy. Iridotomy eliminates pupillary block and reduces the risk for further synechial closure in these eyes. On the other hand, iridotomy is unlikely to help in an eye that already has extensive permanent synechial angle closure.
Primary open-angle glaucoma, steroid-induced glaucoma, and pigmentary glaucoma are all open-angle glaucomas in which indentation gonioscopy is not necessary to assess the angle.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What lens provides a direct gonioscopic view?
pool.rationale: Direct gonioscopy is performed with a binocular microscope, a fiber-optic illuminator or slit-pen light, and a direct goniolens (eg, the Koeppe, Barkan, Wurst, Swan-Jacob, or Richardson lens). This type of lens is often used during examination under anesthesia in the operating room. Indirect gonioscopy is performed more commonly in the clinician's office with lenses that utilize mirrors (eg, the Goldmann, Posner, Sussman, or Zeiss lens).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: After a Trabectome procedure, aqueous humor has direct access to what space?
pool.rationale:
The Trabectome (MicroSurgical Technologies) ablates the trabecular meshwork and allows aqueous to directly access the Schlemm canal.
The subconjunctival space is used in devices such as the XEN Gel Stent (Allergan) and PreserFlo Microshunt (formerly called InnFocus Microshunt; Santen Inc.). Currently, there are no devices approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to shunt aqueous into the suprachoroidal space.
Aqueous drainage devices drain aqueous humor from the anterior chamber to the sub-Tenon space.
The hyaloid canal runs from the optic nerve to the lens and is not involved in aqueous flow.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient is found to have a cup-to-disk (C/D) ratio of 0.8 in both eyes in the setting of normal intraocular pressure (IOP) and no visual field defects. What is the best description of the findings in this patient?
pool.rationale:
A glaucoma suspect is defined as an individual with one or more of these findings:
  • a suspicious optic nerve or nerve fiber layer appearance in the absence of a visual field defect
  • a visual field defect suggestive of glaucoma in the absence of a corresponding glaucomatous optic nerve abnormality
  • a family history of glaucoma in a first-degree relative
  • elevated IOP without evidence of optic nerve damage
Normal tension glaucoma would have corresponding optic nerve and visual field defects in the setting of normal IOP. Ocular hypertension is elevated IOP (usually arbitrarily defined as greater than 21 mm Hg) in the setting of normal optic nerves and visual fields. Primary open-angle glaucoma would usually include elevated IOP along with optic nerve and visual field abnormalities in the setting of an open angle.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What aqueous shunt is a valved device?
pool.rationale:
Aqueous shunts can be categorized as valved or nonvalved. Nonvalved devices require flow restriction in the early postoperative period, until encapsulation of the plate occurs.
Valved devices include the Ahmed and Krupin valves, although currently, the Krupin valve is rarely used.
The Molteno and Baerveldt are commonly used nonvalved implants. The Schocket implant consists of an anterior chamber tube shunt connected to an encircling band; this device is not in common use. A variation of the Schocket implant is angiocatheter tubing that connects the anterior chamber to the capsule surrounding a previously placed scleral buckle.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What did the EAGLE study suggest in regard to certain patients with primary angle closure and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP?

options.a: Patients benefit more from lens extraction than LPI/medical therapy.
options.b: Patients benefit most from treatment with both laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) and lens extraction.
options.c: Patients benefit equally from either LPI or lens extraction.
options.d: Patients benefit most from only medical therapy.

pool.rationale: The EAGLE Study was a prospective controlled randomized trial that studied the efficacy of lens extraction (without visually significant cataract) in the setting of primary angle closure (PAC) and elevated IOP.  The control group in the study received LPI plus medications as needed. Results showed that the lens extraction group had lower IOP, less medication usage, better quality of life, and similar rates of visual field (VF) progression compared to the control group. While there may be some controversy, it appears that in the setting of elevated IOP (≥30 mm Hg) and PAC, lensectomy may be the preferred option of treatment, versus LPI +/- medications.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with progressive visual field loss in the absence of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), what is the initial IOP-percentage lowering goal?
pool.rationale: IOP-lowering goals in normal-tension glaucoma are guided by results of the Collaborative Normal-Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS). The CNTGS found that lowering IOP by at least 30% reduced the 5-year risk of visual field progression from 35% to 12%, proving that intraocular pressure plays a role in normal-tension glaucoma. Since many patients in the untreated group did not progress in the first 5 years of the study, it may be reasonable to initially follow a patient for progression. Once progression is confirmed, an appropriate initial target IOP is 30% lower from peak baseline.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Three months after a vitreous hemorrhage, an intraocular pressure of 35 mm Hg is measured. The angle is open and abundant tan-colored cells are observed in the anterior chamber with a trace amount of flare. What are these cells most likely to be?
pool.rationale:
Ghost-cell glaucoma occurs in association with vitreous hemorrhage. Red blood cells (RBCs) degenerate in the vitreous, migrate forward to the anterior chamber (AC) through a disrupted anterior hyaloid face (usually due to vitrectomy, cataract surgery, or trauma), and then obstruct the trabecular meshwork. The degenerated RBCs appear as tan-colored spheres known as ghost cells, which contain clumps of denatured hemoglobin. Ghost cells are more rigid than normal RBCs and therefore do not pass as easily through the trabecular meshwork. On slit-lamp exam, ghost cells are seen in the vitreous, AC, and trabecular meshwork. Sometimes, the cells are numerous enough to resemble a hypopyon. The cells are eventually cleared by the trabecular meshwork; therefore, initial management is medical. In refractory cases, AC washout with or without vitrectomy might be required.
Hemolytic glaucoma is similar to ghost cell glaucoma except that in hemolytic glaucoma, macrophages phagocytize RBC debris and then occlude the trabecular meshwork. The macrophages appear as reddish cells in the aqueous and the trabecular meshwork has a reddish-brown discoloration.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What tube shunt was evaluated in the Tube Versus Trabeculectomy (TVT) Study?
pool.rationale:
2

The TVT Study was a multicenter randomized clinical trial that evaluated 212 eyes of 212 patients at 17 clinical centers. Patients were randomized as to tube shunt (Baerveldt 350 mm2) or trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C. In a 5-year follow-up study, results showed that tube shunt surgery had a higher success rate compared to trabeculectomy with mitomycin-C; both procedures were associated with a similar reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP).
Main outcome measures included: IOP, visual acuity, use of supplemental medical therapy, and failure (IOP >21 mm Hg or not reduced by 20%, IOP ≤5 mm Hg, reoperation for glaucoma, or loss of light perception vision).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 72-year-old woman who had a central retinal vein occlusion in her left eye presents with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 39 mm Hg and has iris and angle neovascularization. She is having severe pain and notes severely decreased vision for several months. Examination shows a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in the left eye and hand motions vision. What is the most appropriate treatment option for the elevated IOP?
pool.rationale:
This patient has neovascular glaucoma (NVG), a relatively common outcome of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). While initial treatment often targets retinal hypoxia, which is the stimulus for neovascularization, by performing panretinal photocoagulation and/or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections, this patient appears to be in advanced stages of NVG. In this case, given the poor visual prognosis, endoscopic or transscleral cyclophotocoagulation (CPC) can be considered as an alternative to filtering surgery/tube shunt implantation for control of elevated IOP. Active NVG will often cause complications during filtering surgery or tube shunt implantation, so these options are not as appropriate in this patient. The lowering of IOP with CPC will likely improve her pain as well.
Medical management of the IOP may be instituted at the same time as treatment for the neovascularization, as a temporizing measure and/or before surgical treatment. Choosing which class(es) of medication to use will depend on the patient's comorbidities and medical history.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of topical glaucoma medication can induce angle closure in patients with phacomorphic narrowing of the angles?
pool.rationale: Miotic agents can induce angle closure by contraction of the ciliary muscle. This causes an increase of the anteroposterior lens diameter. An increase in this diameter in turn increases lens-iris contact, which can lead to pupillary block glaucoma. Patients with large lenses (phacomorphic narrowing) are particularly susceptible to this, as they already have a degree of lens-iris contact.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For what surgical glaucoma procedure is the degree of intraocular pressure lowering not affected by episcleral venous pressure?
pool.rationale: Procedures that bypass the conventional outflow system, such as trabeculectomy and tube shunts, are not affected by episcleral venous pressure. In contrast, canaloplasty, trabectome, and iStent are all designed to improve transtrabecular flow to increase conventional outflow and would therefore be affected by episcleral venous pressure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How does selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) differ from argon laser trabeculoplasty (ALT)?

options.a: SLT effects persist for longer than ALT.
options.b: SLT lowers IOP to a greater degree than ALT.
options.c: SLT causes more tissue damage than ALT.
options.d: SLT delivers less energy than ALT.

pool.rationale: SLT delivers less energy than ALT. SLT is based on the principle of selective photothermolysis targeting pigmented cells. The laser is applied in short, low-energy bursts that are absorbed selectively by pigmented trabecular meshwork cells with little damage to surrounding tissue. With SLT, there is histologically less damage to the tissue, and several studies have shown that the efficacy of SLT and ALT are equivalent. Just as with argon laser trabeculoplasty, the effect of selective laser trabeculoplasty tends to diminish over time.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Endocyclophotocoagulation uses thermal energy to decrease aqueous production from the ciliary processes. What cells are the source of aqueous production in the eye?
pool.rationale: The inner nonpigmented epithelial cells are believed to be the actual site of aqueous production. The ciliary body contains approximately 80 ciliary processes composed of an outer pigmented and inner nonpigmented later of epithelial cells that face each other at their apical surfaces and are joined together by tight junctions. These tight junctions are one component of the blood-aqueous barrier. The double layer of epithelium surrounds a rich supply of fenestrated capillaries at the core of each ciliary process, and the inner nonpigmented epithelial cells contain numerous mitochondria and microvilli, providing the energy to produce the aqueous. The inner nonpigmented epithelial cells protrude into the posterior chamber and are in direct contact with the endocyclophotocoagulation laser during treatment. The protrusions of the microvilli of the nonpigmented epithelial cells provide a large surface area for aqueous secretion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with recurrent, unilateral uveitis has pain, photophobia, and 2+ anterior chamber cells. Despite 3 weeks of topical corticosteroid therapy, the patient has persistent 1+ anterior chamber cells. On examination, IOP is 37 mm Hg, and the optic nerve appears similar to that of the contralateral, non-inflamed eye. What is the recommended next step in management?
pool.rationale: Elevation of IOP associated with uveitis can be related to trabecular inflammation, cellular trabecular obstruction, corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension, and occlusio pupillae with synechial angle closure. The preferred initial treatment is the addition of an aqueous suppressant. A common clinical management dilemma develops when corticosteroids may be the cause of elevated IOP. The primary goal of uveitis management is to suppress ocular inflammation. In the presence of active inflammation, anti-inflammatory therapy must be continued. While weaker steroid formulations are less likely to raise IOP, they are also less effective at controlling inflammation, and substitution should only be considered when the inflammation is suppressed. The addition of an aqueous suppressant such as a beta blocker or carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is an effective initial option when corticosteroid therapy must be continued. If topical medications fail and IOP remains chronically elevated, surgical intervention may be necessary; however, this is ideally performed when the eye is not inflamed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What blood vessels principally supply the superficial nerve fiber layer of the optic disc?

options.a: branches of the circle of Zinn-Haller
options.b: recurrent retinal arterioles branching from the central retinal artery
options.c: branches from the short posterior ciliary arteries

pool.rationale:
Recurrent retinal arterioles branching from the central retinal artery principally supply the superficial nerve fiber layer of the optic disc. These vessels are known as epipapillary vessels, and they originate from the peripapillary nerve fiber layer and course toward the center of the optic disc.
The prelaminar and laminar regions of the optic nerve are supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries and branches of the circle of Zinn-Haller. The retrolaminar region of the optic nerve is supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries and the pial arteries. Also, the central retinal artery may supply a few small intraneural branches in the retrolaminar area.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient on topiramate therapy presents with bilateral acute angle-closure glaucoma. First-line management consists of discontinuation of topiramate, administration of ocular hypotensive medications, and what other therapy?
pool.rationale: Sulfamate-substituted monosaccharide medications, such as topiramate, can cause an idiosyncratic reaction leading to bilateral acute myopia and angle closure. There may also be associated anterior segment inflammation. Ultrasound biomicroscopy usually shows ciliochoroidal swelling with anterior rotation of the ciliary body. First-line treatment includes cycloplegia, hypotensive agents, and discontinuation of the offending agent. In these cases, there is no component of pupillary block so laser iridotomy is not useful. In cases refractory to topiramate discontinuation, laser iridoplasty has been reported to be effective in relieving the angle closure. The ciliary edema is not relieved by choroidal drainage or use of oral prednisone.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In an emmetropic eye, what lens causes the least change in magnification?
pool.rationale: Optic disc size plays an important role in the evaluation of glaucoma. In patients with large discs, a large cup may be physiologic. On the other hand, a cup-disc ratio of 0.5 may be pathologic in a small disc. In this technique, understanding the magnification of the lens being utilized is important. With a 60.00 D lens, the height of the slit equals the disc diameter, in millimeters, read directly from the scale. If a 78.00 D lens is used, the scale reading is multiplied by 1.1, and with a 90.00 D lens, multiplication by 1.3 results in the disc diameter in millimeters. The normal-sized optic nerve head ranges from approximately 1.5 to 2.2 mm in diameter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents 1 month after routine phacoemulsification with elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and focal edema of the inferior cornea. The anterior chamber (AC) is deep with 1+ cell. What is the most likely etiology of this presentation?
pool.rationale:
Aqueous misdirection, lens particle glaucoma, and retained viscoelastic glaucoma are all potential causes of increased intraocular pressure following cataract extraction. After intraocular surgery, different viscoelastic materials vary in the length of time they remain in the eye, based on dispersive and cohesive properties, but all would be expected to be cleared within a few days to a week. Aqueous misdirection (ciliary block, malignant glaucoma) is characterized by a shallow central and peripheral anterior chamber.
Clinical findings in lens particle glaucoma include cortical material in the anterior chamber, elevated IOP, moderate anterior chamber reaction, microcystic corneal edema, and, with time, posterior synechiae and peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
Phacolytic glaucoma is a cause of elevated intraocular pressure (30-50 mm Hg is not uncommon) in older, phakic patients with a mature, hypermature, or morgagnian cataract. High molecular weight lens proteins leak through an intact capsule, causing acute or subacute signs and symptoms (microcystic corneal edema, cell and flare, and/or hypopyon without keratic precipitates (Figures 1 and 2), conjunctival hyperemia (Figure 3) with sudden onset of pain, open-angle on gonioscopy). Aqueous tap reveals macrophages containing lens material (Figure 4).





(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) after laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK), what contact tonometer is most independent of the influence of altered central cornea thickness (CCT)?
pool.rationale:
The DCT is a contact tonometer that is less influenced by CCT. Although it is a contact tonometer, it contours to the cornea, as opposed to applanating it. The shell matching the corneal contour receives signals from the transcoronal forces generated against it and measures IOP at diastole and at systole. Between 5 and 8 cardiac cycles are needed to get a good reading. Diastolic IOP and ocular pulse amplitude (the difference between systolic and diastolic IOP) are displayed. This method has been shown to give similar IOP readings pre- and post-LASIK.
The Perkins tonometer is a hand-held tonometer that uses a 3.06 mm tip diameter with a biprism similar to the slit lamp mounted Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT). The Tono-Pen (Reichert Ophthalmic Instruments, Depew, New York) is a hand-held tonometer that contains a strain gauge and produces an electrical signal as the tip applanates a smaller area of the cornea than the GAT. Since both the Perkins tonometer and the Tono-Pen applanate the cornea, they are similarly influenced by CCT as the GAT.
The iCare (Revenio Corporation, Vantaa, Finland) rebound tonometer is a hand-held tonometer with a magnetized probe that impacts the cornea and then decelerates and rebounds. The probe generates a voltage proportional to speed and direction; this voltage is monitored by a sensor and converted to an IOP value. Reduction of CCT after LASIK has been shown to have a greater effect on rebound tonometry than Goldmann tonometry.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with bilateral posterior embryotoxon, broad iris adhesions to the posterior cornea, and elevated IOP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: This patient has Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, an autosomal dominantly inherited condition associated with bilateral anterior segment anomalies. Characteristic findings include posterior embryotoxon, hypoplastic iris, corectopia, and broad iris adhesions to the embryotoxon. Systemic manifestations include microdontia, maxillary hypoplasia, redundant periumbilical skin, and hypospadias. About 50% of patients go on to develop glaucoma that can be difficult to control. Characteristic anterior segment findings in aniridia are varying absence of iris tissue, limbal stem cell deficiency leading to corneal pannus, and cataract. In neurofibromatosis, a slit-lamp examination can reveal Lisch nodules on the iris. In Peters anomaly, there is a central corneal leukoma that can be associated with iris and/or lens adhesions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A young myopic patient undergoes an uncomplicated trabeculectomy with adjunctive mitomycin C. One month after surgery, the eye is comfortable but the IOP is 8 mm Hg and the best corrected visual acuity has fallen from 20/30 to 20/400. The incision is Seidel-negative. What is the most likely exam finding in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
Visual decline after trabeculectomy can occur as a result of a number of different mechanisms. Young myopic patients are at particular risk of vision loss secondary to hypotony maculopathy even at intraocular pressure levels that one would not commonly associate with this complication. Suprachoroidal hemorrhage is nearly always associated with pain. A cataract can progress after filtering surgery, but the time course is typically more protracted and refractive or pinhole correction should improve the visual acuity. Delayed vitreous hemorrhage in the setting of an uncomplicated trabeculectomy is very uncommon.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with sickle cell disease is hit in the eye with a baseball. On examination, he has a 10% layered hyphema and the intraocular pressure (IOP) is 28 mm Hg. What treatment should be avoided?
pool.rationale:
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) are known to lower the pH of the aqueous, which can induce sickling of red blood cells, preventing clearance through the trabecular meshwork. Systemic CAIs should not be used in patients with sickle cell disease, because there is a risk of sickle cell crisis in sickle cell anemia and an increased risk of formation of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate renal stones.
Although topical CAIs have not been proven to induce anterior chamber acidosis, it may be prudent to use them as a last-line topical agent. Patients with sickle cell hemoglobinopathy are at higher risk for complications associated with traumatic hyphema. They may develop elevated IOP in the presence of microhyphema alone and are at risk for nerve damage with short durations of IOP elevation. All African American patients with a traumatic hyphema should have a sickle prep if their sickle cell status is unknown. Timolol, atropine, and prednisolone acetate 1% do not induce sickling. They can all be used safely for the treatment of hyphema in a sickle cell patient.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the typical angle appearance on gonioscopy in primary congenital glaucoma?

options.b: deep chamber with heavy trabecular meshwork (TM) pigmentation
options.c: deep chamber with iris adhesions to the Schwalbe line
options.d: deep chamber with high iris insertion

pool.rationale: Infants with primary congenital glaucoma typically have deep anterior chambers with a high, flat anterior iris insertion. The peripheral iris may be hypoplastic. Iris adhesions and a prominent embryotoxon may be seen with Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. A heavily pigmented TM may be seen in pigmentary glaucoma but is not a feature of any infantile glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Where should the laser be focused in argon laser trabeculoplasty (ALT)?

options.a: junction of anterior (nonpigmented) and posterior (pigmented) trabecular meshwork
options.b: junction of the Schwalbe line and anterior (nonpigmented) trabecular meshwork
options.c: junction of scleral spur and pigmented trabecular meshwork

pool.rationale: The spot size of SLT is large (400 microns) and is often covering most of the angle structures, compared with that of ALT, which should be adjusted to 50 microns and is aimed toward the junction of the nonpigmented and the pigmented trabecular meshwork. The duration time for SLT is very short (0.3 ns) compared with that of ALT (0.1 seconds). SLT targets intracellular melanin and is considered less destructive compared with ALT, and therefore it can be repeated several times in the same eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: One week after trabeculectomy, a patient complains of blurry vision. Intraocular pressure is 3 mm Hg. Exam shows a large bleb, a deep anterior chamber, and macular choroidal folds. What other fundus finding is most likely?
pool.rationale: The clinical description provided is consistent with hypotony maculopathy. This complication of overfiltration is more common in young myopes, whereas choroidal detachments are more common in older patients. The fundus findings of hypotony maculopathy include optic disc edema, macular folds, and cystoid macular edema. Although both choroidal detachment and hypotony maculopathy are findings associated with ocular hypotony, they do not typically occur simultaneously. In addition, choroidal detachment is usually associated with a shallow anterior chamber. Intraretinal hemorrhages can be seen in decompression retinopathy. Vitreous hemorrhage is an uncommon complication of trabeculectomy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), what percentage of untreated patients progressed to glaucoma during a 5-year period?
pool.rationale: The OHTS assessed the efficacy of topical ocular hypotensive medications in preventing or delaying the onset of visual field loss in ocular hypertension. Treated groups had an IOP reduction of 22.5% vs an IOP decrease of 4% in control groups. In the treated group, 4.4% developed optic nerve or visual field damage over 5 years. In the untreated group, 9.5% developed optic nerve or visual field damage in 5 years. The study also showed that for each millimeter of mercury (mm Hg) elevated above baseline IOP, the risk of progression increased by 10%. Similarly, for each 0.1 increment in vertical C/D ratio, the risk of progression increased by 32%.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of hyperosmotic agents such as glycerol and mannitol?

options.a: resultant renal metabolic acidosis, which reduces activity of ciliary epithelial function
options.d: contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle fibers that insert in the trabecular meshwork

pool.rationale: Hyperosmotic agents such as mannitol and glycerol dehydrate the vitreous and decrease intraocular fluid volume by osmotically drawing fluid into the intravascular space. They are given either orally or intravenously and are often useful in cases of acute angle closure glaucoma refractory to other medications. They are contraindicated in patients with congestive heart failure, diabetic ketoacidosis (glycerin), subdural or subarachnoid hemorrhage, and preexisting severe dehydration.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the anatomic significance of the corneal optical wedge in gonioscopy?

options.a: the boundary between the non-pigmented and pigmented trabecular meshwork
options.c: the anterior insertion of the longitudinal ciliary muscle
options.d: the origin of the aqueous collector channels

pool.rationale: The corneal optical wedge is found at the posterior termination of Descemet membrane and the corneal endothelium. It is the most anterior structure of the anterior chamber angle and can be used in cases of challenging anatomy to orient the examiner. The longitudinal ciliary muscle inserts anteriorly onto the scleral spur. The boundary between the anterior non-pigmented and posterior pigmented trabecular meshwork does not have a commonly used name, although the Schlemm canal can be found deep to this location. The aqueous collector channels originate from the circumferential the Schlemm canal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What component of the trabecular meshwork (TM) is targeted when applying treatment with selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT)?

options.c: endothelial cells of the Schlemm canal

pool.rationale: While the various components of the trabecular meshwork including the extracellular matrix, the endothelial cells of the Schlemm canal, and/or the juxtacanalicular cells, may be affected by SLT and are theorized to change in response to the treatment to increase outflow, none of these components are directly targeted during the treatment. SLT targets intracellular melanin for uptake, with the resultant effects on various parts of the trabecular meshwork. Phagocytic cells in the TM may also be activated by SLT and help increase outflow as a result of the treatment, but the mechanism of action of SLT is not fully understood.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: By what mechanism do Rho kinase inhibitors lower intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale:
Rho kinase inhibitors (eg, netarsudil) increase trabecular outflow by increasing phosphorylation and activation of the protein myosin light chain (MLC) phosphatase. Phosphorylated MLC then interacts with actin to affect the physical properties of the cytoskeleton, resulting in relaxation of the cytoskeleton of outflow cells in the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm canal, allowing for increased aqueous outflow.
Prostaglandin analogues (eg, latanoprost) lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow and decreasing outflow resistance. Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, dorzolamide), beta blockers (eg, timolol), and alpha-2 agonists (eg, brimonidine) decrease aqueous humor production. Hyperosmotic agents (eg, mannitol) increase blood osmolality, thus creating an osmotic gradient to draw water from the eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What tonometer type provides a measurement of corneal hysteresis?
pool.rationale:
The ocular response analyzer (ORA) is a noncontact tonometer that utilizes a soft and rapid air puff and records 2 applanation pressure measurements, the first measuring the force required to flatten the cornea with pressure rise, and the second measuring the fall in air pressure when the cornea rebounds. The difference between the 2 values is termed corneal hysteresis: measuring the biomechanical property of the cornea. This measurement may influence interpretation of intraocular tensions, similarly to central corneal thickness and corneal curvature.
The dynamic contour tonometer is a noninvasive contact method for measuring intraocular pressure after refractive surgical procedures; the measurements are unaffected by corneal biomechanics. Rebound tonometry measures the speed at which a small probe propelled against the cornea decelerates and rebounds after impact. Topical anesthetic is not required.
The pneumotonometer makes contact with only a small area of the cornea. It is useful in eyes with corneal scars or edema. Measurements obtained by placing the probe on the sclera appear to correlate well with those obtained with the probe placed on the cornea, suggesting that it can be used to monitor IOP in patients with keratoprostheses.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of ocular hypotensive agents is associated with the development of apnea in infants and young children?
pool.rationale: α2-selective adrenergic agonists have been reported to cause severe, life-threatening apnea, central nervous system depression, and bradycardia in infants and children. These agents can cross the blood-brain barrier, particularly in infants. They are contraindicated for use in young children and should be avoided in nursing mothers.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What side effect is typically associated with prostaglandin analogues?
pool.rationale: Prostaglandin analogues are very well tolerated as a class of hypotensive medications. Local side effects are most common and include conjunctival hyperemia, hypertrichosis, and increased pigmentation of the iris and periocular skin. Less commonly, these drugs have been associated with cystoid macular edema, anterior uveitis, and reactivation of herpes simplex virus keratitis. While systemic side effects are not frequent, flu-like symptoms and joint/muscle pains can occur. Bitter taste is often associated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, decreased exercise tolerance is typically associated with beta-blockers, and dry mouth is associated with alpha-agonists.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action by which the parasympathomimetic agents reduce intraocular pressure (IOP)?

options.a: longitudinal ciliary muscle fiber contraction with increased outflow through the trabecular meshwork
options.b: circular ciliary muscle fiber relaxation with increased outflow through the trabecular meshwork
options.c: longitudinal ciliary muscle fiber relaxation with increased outflow through the trabecular meshwork
options.d: circular ciliary muscle fiber contraction with increased outflow through the trabecular meshwork

pool.rationale: Parasympathomimetic agents, or miotics, reduce the IOP by causing contraction of the longitudinal ciliary muscle fibers where they insert into the scleral spur and trabecular meshwork. This contraction in turn improves outflow. There are 2 types of parasympathomimetic agents: direct-acting and indirect-acting agents. Direct-acting agents mimic acetylcholine at postganglionic parasympathetic junctions and other autonomic, somatic, and central synapses. Indirect-acting agents prolong and enhance the action of secreted acetylcholine at the junctions. Pilocarpine, the most commonly used parasympathomimetic agent, is available in percentages of 1%, 2%, and 4%. It has been shown to reduce the IOP by 15% to 20%.

pool.q: A patient with a history of an occludable angle and glaucoma in his right eye is now 3 years status-post cataract surgery. On gonioscopy scleral spur is visible in 4/4 quadrants. His treated intraocular pressure (IOP) has been in the mid 20s on several visits, and he demonstrates visual field, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and optic nerve changes consistent with progression of his disease over the past year. What is the most accurate classification of this patient's glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
This patient's history of occludable angles and prior glaucoma suggests a component of angle-closure glaucoma in his history. Now, after cataract surgery, the patient has an anatomically open angle. However, his treated pressure continues to be elevated, with evidence of glaucomatous progression, suggesting persistently reduced outflow facility. As such, the most accurate classification of his glaucoma is combined mechanism, because he seems to have progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy despite anatomic correction of the occludable angle and he has persistently elevated IOP. Combined-mechanism glaucoma can also be used to refer to glaucoma in which several mechanisms are at play, for example primary open-angle glaucoma with superimposed neovascular glaucoma or primary open-angle glaucoma with a superimposed corticosteroid response or uveitic component.
Primary open-angle glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which there is no physical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork visible at the gonioscopic level, and there is no underlying abnormality accounting for the condition.
Secondary open-angle glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which a secondary condition (eg, corticosteroid-induced IOP elevation) accounts for impaired aqueous outflow in the setting of an anatomically open angle.
Primary angle-closure glaucoma refers to glaucoma in which there is partial or complete obstruction of the angle by peripheral iris, either appositional or synechial, in the absence of an underlying condition.

pool.q: What type of glaucoma is associated with a higher risk for post-trabeculectomy hypotony maculopathy?
pool.rationale: Risk factors for hypotony maculopathy include young age and myopia, both of which are typical characteristics of patients with pigmentary glaucoma. Judicious use of antimetabolites and placement of additional and/or tighter scleral flap sutures are advisable in patients with this type of glaucoma. The other types of glaucoma listed (pseudoexfoliative, angle-recession, steroid-induced) are not associated with a higher risk of hypotony maculopathy after trabeculectomy.

pool.q: What is the most likely cause of elevated intraocular pressure in pseudoexfoliation glaucoma?

options.a: fibrillar material inducing peripheral anterior synechiae
options.b: fibrillar material obstructing the trabecular meshwork
options.c: fibrillar material deposited on zonules with anterior rotation lens
options.d: fibrillar material causing hypersecretion from the ciliary body

pool.rationale: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is thought to cause intraocular pressure elevation by obstruction of flow through, and damage to the trabecular meshwork or the uveoscleral pathway from direct fibrillar material deposition. Hypersecretion, pupillary block, and synechial closure of the angle are not the most common mechanisms of elevated intraocular pressure in pseudoexfoliation glaucoma.

pool.q: Two days after an eye with chronic retinal detachment and proliferative vitreoretinopathy has undergone pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil injection, the intraocular pressure (IOP) is 50 mm Hg on maximal medical therapy and iris bombé is noted. What is the most appropriate next step?
pool.rationale:
Intravitreal silicone oil (SO) is causing pupillary block and secondary angle closure with IOP elevation. The pupillary block should be relieved by an iridotomy. Because SO has a lower specific gravity than water and floats in the vitreous cavity, a superior iridotomy will be obstructed by SO. Therefore, an inferior iridotomy should be created.
Removal of SO is not indicated in this patient, because there is a risk of retinal redetachment.
Cyclophotocoagulation is not indicated as the first intervention in this eye.

pool.q: What form of contact tonometry does not require topical anesthetic?
pool.rationale: Both iCare (Revenio Corporation, Vantaa, Finland) tonometry and ORA do not require anesthesia. iCare is a contact tonometer and ORA is a noncontact tonometer. DCT and pneumotonometry require prolonged corneal contact, necessitating topical anesthesia.

pool.q: During gonioscopy of a Shaffer Grade 4 open angle, what structure is seen most anteriorly?
pool.rationale:
The Schwalbe line is the termination of Descemet membrane and is the most anterior angle landmark. Its location can be confirmed with the parallelepiped or corneal light wedge technique.
In a Shaffer Grade 4 open angle, the structures visible from anterior to posterior on gonioscopy are cornea, Schwalbe line, nonpigmented trabecular meshwork, pigmented trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, anterior face of ciliary body, and iris root.

pool.q: Thinner central corneal thickness is a risk factor for glaucomatous progression. In what glaucoma clinical trial was this first identified?
pool.rationale: The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS) was designed to determine the effectiveness of topical ocular hypotensives in preventing or delaying the onset of glaucoma in patients with ocular hypertension. Thinner central corneal thickness, older age, high intraocular pressure (IOP), larger cup-to-disc (C/D) ratio, and worse pattern standard deviation on visual field testing were all identified as risk factors for the conversion to glaucoma. This trial was pivotal in identifying the importance of measuring central corneal thickness in glaucoma evaluations.

pool.q: A 76-year-old woman has pseudoexfoliation syndrome, a visually significant cataract, and iridodonesis on examination. What problem is this patient most likely to have at the time of cataract surgery?
pool.rationale: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is a common cause of zonular weakness. Iridodonesis at the time of slit-lamp examination may be a signal of zonular weakness. Focal weakness or absence of the posterior lens capsule is associated with a posterior polar cataract. Reverse pupillary block is associated with high myopia. Positive pressure inside the capsular bag is associated with an intumescent cataract.

pool.q: A patient with plateau iris syndrome is prescribed pilocarpine drops to prevent angle closure. What dosing is recommended?
pool.rationale: Use of pilocarpine in this setting requires 3 to 4 times daily dosing, and the other dosing schedules listed would not be adequate. Pilocarpine is a parasympathomimetic agent that historically has been used for glaucoma treatment. Long-term use of pilocarpine has fallen out of favor due to the frequency of dosing required, along with its adverse effects, but it is still used in certain circumstances, such as in patients with occludable angles despite a patent laser peripheral iridotomy (ie, plateau iris syndrome).

pool.q: What is the underlying mechanism of plateau iris syndrome?
pool.rationale: Plateau iris configuration is a narrow angle caused by anteriorly positioned ciliary processes that push the peripheral iris forward. In plateau iris syndrome, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and angle closure develop despite a patent iridotomy. Anterior iris insertions are often seen in anterior chamber developmental anomalies and congenital glaucoma. Anterior iris rotation may cause angle closure in aniridia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Progression of what corneal disease warrants discontinuation of topical dorzolamide?
pool.rationale:
Use of topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs), including dorzolamide, in the setting of compromised endothelial cell function can place patients at risk for corneal decompensation. For this reason, topical CAIs should be used with caution in patients with Fuchs corneal endothelial dystrophy.
Keratoconus, lattice degeneration of the cornea, and Terrien marginal degeneration are all not associated with endothelial compromise.
