pool.q: A 69-year-old man with glaucoma presents with blurry vision in both eyes. Best corrected visual acuity is 20/200 OD and 20/150 OS. Intraocular pressure (IOP) is 12 mm Hg OD and 10 mm Hg OS on a prostaglandin analog OU QHS, dorzolamide and timolol OU BID, and brimonidine OU BID. Anterior segment evaluation reveals 3+ nuclear sclerosis OU and gonioscopy shows open angles OU. Both eyes have advanced cupping. The patient understands that part of his vision loss is due to cataract and wants cataract surgery. What is the preferred surgical procedure in this patient?

options.a: Combined cataract and glaucoma surgery is appropriate for this patient.
options.b: Glaucoma surgery alone is appropriate for this patient.
options.c: The patient is at high risk for vision loss and should not have cataract surgery.
options.d: Cataract surgery alone is appropriate for this patient.

pool.rationale:
Combined cataract and glaucoma surgery is the appropriate choice for this patient, who has advanced optic nerve cupping and is on maximum topical therapy for glaucoma.
Cataract surgery alone is not recommended, because even a transient postoperative IOP spike can cause further damage in this patient who has advanced glaucomatous cupping.
Glaucoma surgery alone will not address the issue of visual impairment due to cataract.
Cataract surgery should not be withheld, because the patient does have the potential for visual improvement, and combining cataract extraction with glaucoma surgery will allow control of IOP in the postoperative period.

pool.q: A 60-year-old African American woman with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is also allergic to benzalkonium chloride (BAK). She uses preservative-free timolol drops, but her intraocular pressure (IOP) is not lowered adequately. What is the next step in managing this patient's condition?
pool.rationale:
BAK is used as a preservative in both brinzolamide and bimatoprost eyedrops; these drops should not be used in a patient with BAK allergy.
LTP is effective in lowering IOP in patients with POAG, pigmentary glaucoma, exfoliation glaucoma, and steroid-induced glaucoma. LTP can be used as primary or adjuvant therapy and is an appropriate choice for this patient.
Laser gonioplasty or iridoplasty is used in the management of primary angle-closure disease and is not indicated in this patient.

pool.q: In what condition are peripheral anterior synechiae most likely to extend past the Schwalbe line?
pool.rationale:
ICE syndrome is caused by an abnormal corneal endothelium that forms a membrane over the anterior surface of the iris and angle structures. Contraction of this membrane results in formation of peripheral anterior synechiae that extend beyond the Schwalbe line onto the corneal endothelium.
Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), seen after argon laser trabeculoplasty, are typically small, do not extend beyond the trabecular meshwork, and correspond to the laser treatment locations.
In A-R syndrome there is an anteriorly displaced prominent Schwalbe line, but PAS seen in this condition attach to the Schwalbe line and do not extend beyond it.
In neovascular glaucoma, contraction of a fibrovascular membrane results in PAS formation and angle closure. The abnormal membrane does not extend beyond the Schwalbe line into normal corneal endothelium.

pool.q: Epidemiologic studies suggest what distribution of intraocular pressure in populations of European ancestry?

options.a: non-Gaussian with skew toward higher pressures
options.b: Gaussian with skew toward lower pressures
options.c: Gaussian with skew toward higher pressures
options.d: non-Gaussian with skew toward lower pressures

pool.rationale: Epidemiologic studies of populations with European-derived ancestry have demonstrated a non-Gaussian distribution of intraocular pressure, with a skew toward higher pressures. This is particularly true in individuals over the age of 40. Pooled data suggests a mean IOP of 15.5 mm Hg in the general population of European ancestry, with a standard deviation of 2.6 mm Hg. The "abnormal" cut off of >21 mm Hg is thus derived from 15.5 + 2 standard deviations, though this is problematic given the non-normal distribution observed and skew toward higher IOP.

pool.q: In what type of glaucoma is a post-laser trabeculoplasty intraocular pressure (IOP) spike most common?
pool.rationale: Patients with heavily pigmented trabecular meshworks are more prone to post-argon laser trabeculoplasty/selective laser trabeculoplasty (post-ALT/SLT) IOP spikes, due to greater absorption of the laser energy. One should use lower power and/or consider treating a smaller area when performing laser trabeculoplasty in pigmentary glaucoma patients. This phenomenon may also occur to a lesser degree with pseudoexfoliation (PXE) patients.

pool.q: What type of tonometer uses the Imbert-Fick principle for measurement of intraocular pressure (IOP)?
pool.rationale: Like the Goldmann tonometer, the Perkins tonometer is an applanation tonometer, and as such, is based on the Imbert-Fick principle. The Imbert-Fick principle relates the pressure inside a dry, thin-walled sphere to the force required to flatten a specific area. The Goldmann applanation tonometer and the Perkins tonometer use the same measurement tip, which balances surface tension of the tear film with the rigidity of the cornea to approximate a dry, infinitely flexible, thin-walled sphere for eyes with corneal thickness of 520 μm.

pool.q: A 50-year-old man has an IOP of 30 mm Hg OD and 26 mm Hg OS. Corneal thickness is 554 OD and 550 OS. The optic nerves have C:D ratios of 0.3 with healthy rims OU, and the visual field and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) are normal OU. The patient’s father has primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). Based on the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), what can this patient be told about his risk for developing glaucoma?

options.a: Most untreated patients do not progress to glaucoma.
options.b: Positive family history is the strongest predictor of developing glaucoma.
options.c: Delaying treatment increases the risk of progression to glaucoma.
options.d: Lowering IOP has no effect on the risk of developing glaucoma.

pool.rationale:
The OHTS was a randomized controlled trial in which participants 40 to 80 years of age with IOPs between 24 mm Hg and 32 mm Hg were randomized to either observation or treatment with topical medications. Over a 5-year period, 4.4% of the treatment group and 9.5% of the untreated group progressed to glaucoma based on visual field and optic nerve changes. Thus, decreasing IOP lowered the risk of progression to glaucoma. However, most untreated patients did not develop glaucoma.
After a median duration of 7.5 years, topical treatment was initiated in the original untreated group and continued for 5.5 years after. Participants in the original treatment group continued medications for a median of 13 years. Results from this follow-up study showed that delaying treatment did not result in an increased risk of conversion to glaucoma.
Family history of glaucoma was not identified as a significant risk factor in the OHTS but this could have been due to inaccurate assessment from self-reporting of this factor. Therefore, clinicians must consider family history when evaluating a patient's risk of developing glaucoma. Central corneal thickness was a powerful predictor of developing glaucoma in the OHTS. There was an 81% increase in relative risk for every 40 μm thinner CCT. Other risk factors were larger C:D ratio at baseline, increased age, higher IOP, and higher PSD on standard automated perimetry.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What topical intraocular pressure lowering therapy should be avoided in patients with reactive airway disease?
pool.rationale: Beta-adrenergic antagonists, including levobunolol, can induce severe bronchospasm in susceptible patients; therefore, a history of asthma is a contraindication to therapy with beta-blockers. Other systemic adverse effects of ß-blockers include bradycardia, increased heart block, lowered blood pressure, reduced exercise tolerance, central nervous system (CNS) depression, masking hypoglycemic signs and symptoms in patients with diabetes, and aggravation of myasthenia gravis. Pilocarpine, latanoprost, and dorzolamide are not contraindicated in patients with reactive airway disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most likely demographic category to present with angle-closure glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Angle closure is more commonly seen in patients with a short axial length or hyperopes. The frequency of this condition is highest among Alaskan and Greenland Inuits and other Asian ethnic groups (Chinese, Southeast Asian, and South Asians from India). In addition, angle-closure glaucoma has a higher prevalence in women.

pool.q: For examination of the optic nerve, what is the main disadvantage of direct ophthalmoscopy compared to slit-lamp biomicroscopy?

options.a: inability to view the nerve fiber layer
options.b: less detailed view of the optic nerve

pool.rationale: The main disadvantage of the direct ophthalmoscope is that the lack of stereopsis can result in subtle optic nerve head details being overlooked. The instrument can, however, be used to examine the disc through a small pupil; the use of a red-free filter enhances visualization of the nerve fiber layer.

pool.q: A 55-year-old Chinese woman presents with intraocular pressures (IOPs) of 40 mm Hg OU. The cup-to-disc ratios are 0.85 and focal thinning of the neuroretinal rim is present in both eyes. What would the most important step in the evaluation be?
pool.rationale:
This patient requires IOP-lowering treatment. Gonioscopy is critical in the evaluation in order to rule out angle closure, which has a higher prevalence in Asian persons than white persons. If angle closure is present, laser iridotomy must be considered in the management plan, along with IOP-lowering medications.
Although pachymetry, visual field testing, and disc imaging all provide useful information, they do not alter the initial management of this patient's condition.

pool.q: What feature is common to all subtypes of iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome?
pool.rationale: ICE syndrome is a group of disorders that includes essential iris atrophy, Chandler syndrome, and Cogan-Reese syndrome. All of these have abnormal endothelial cells with a "beaten bronze" appearance on slit-lamp examination. ICE syndrome is more common in women and commonly presents between 20 and 50 years of age. The condition is isolated to the eye, and is sporadic and unilateral.

pool.q: A 75-year-old white man presents with newly diagnosed glaucoma and an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 23 mm Hg. His cup-to-disc ratio is 0.5 OD, with an early inferior notch and with corresponding early superior arcuate changes on his visual field in the right eye. What should the initial IOP reduction be?
pool.rationale: The initial target IOP range is individualized based on factors such as IOP level at which optic nerve damage occurred or is believed to have occurred, severity of disc damage, patient age, and life expectancy of the patient. An initial IOP reduction of at least 20% from baseline is recommended, and the range of 20%-30% is commonly used. In this patient, IOP lowering of 25% from baseline is appropriate given the clinical findings, which do not indicate severe glaucomatous damage. Further follow-up determines whether this level of IOP lowering is adequate or not; if disease progression continues, further IOP lowering may be required.

pool.q: What type of primary angle closure (PAC) occurs independently of pupillary block?
pool.rationale: Elevation of IOP occurs with plateau iris syndrome without pupillary block or its characteristic iris profile. Plateau iris syndrome can develop even in the setting of a patent iridotomy. The other forms of PAC given develop from a pupillary block mechanism.

pool.q: A 66-year-old woman presents with normal intraocular pressure (IOP). She describes intermittent haloes and headaches on the left side, around her eye, that resolve with sleep. Her primary care physician has told her he suspects migraine headache. What is the best next step to assist in diagnosis?

options.d: assessment of pupillary response to light

pool.rationale:
This patient is complaining of symptoms often seen with intermittently elevated IOP caused by subacute/intermittent angle closure. The resolution with sleep is due to sleep-induced miosis. This condition is often misdiagnosed as migraine-type headache.
The best next step in workup and diagnosis is to assess the angle with gonioscopy. The other clinical assessments, such as optic nerve imaging and neuroimaging, may be necessary, but not at this point in the clinical examination of the patient. Pupillary light response is important as part of a general examination but will not provide any specific information about intermittent angle closure.

pool.q: What type of prior eye surgery may result in an underestimation of intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale: In a patient suspected to have normal-tension glaucoma, it is important to ask about other factors that could cause intraocular pressure to be higher than what is measured in clinic. Refractive surgery may result in decreased corneal thickness, which can result in an underestimation of intraocular pressure, and a seemingly normal IOP. Cataract surgery and pars plana vitrectomy do not result in underestimation of intraocular pressure. It has. however, been posited that scleral buckling might change IOP measurement as a result of changes in corneal hysteresis. Refractive surgery remains the "best" answer.

pool.q: What condition may cause an artificially low intraocular pressure (IOP) reading with Goldmann applanation tonometry?
pool.rationale: Corneal edema may result in an artificially low IOP measurement. Breath holding (or Valsalva), excess fluorescein with thick mires, band keratopathy (corneal scarring), and high corneal astigmatism can all produce artificially high IOP measurements obtained with Goldmann tonometry.

pool.q: A patient whose intraocular pressure (IOP) is 36 mm Hg in one eye is referred by a retinal specialist to another ophthalmologist. The patient has history of exudative age-related macular degeneration and has been receiving intravitreal injections of bevacizumab for the past several years in that eye. No treatment to lower the IOP has been initiated yet. What is the best therapeutic option at this time for that purpose?
pool.rationale: While the exact mechanism for IOP elevation remains unknown, there is a noted association in the literature between multiple anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections and chronic elevated IOP. Theories include inflammation and/or blockage of the trabecular meshwork. Based on this, the mechanism appears to be a secondary open-angle glaucoma; therefore, treatment with LPI would not be appropriate. Surgical therapy may be indicated in these patients if the IOP cannot be controlled medically and/or there are other contraindications to medical treatment. Generally, topical therapy is instituted before systemic therapy when attempting to lower IOP, because there is less potential for side effects.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What medication is most likely to cause prolonged intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation following intravitreal administration?
pool.rationale:
Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid and is most likely to caused prolonged intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation after intravitreal injection. The mechanism of IOP elevation is reduction in outflow facility by accumulation of glycosaminoglycans in the trabecular meshwork (TM) and reduction of TM phagocytic activity. The risk of corticosteroid-induced increase in IOP is highest with periocular or intraocular injection.
Intravitreal injection of the other listed medications (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and ceftazidime) may cause an immediate increase in IOP due to expanded vitreous volume. Sustained IOP elevation has been reported with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents but is not as common as with triamcinolone.

pool.q: Open-angle glaucoma causes loss of what tissue layer(s) of the retina?

options.a: nerve fiber layer and inner nuclear layer
options.b: outer nuclear layer and photoreceptor layer
options.d: nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell layer

pool.rationale:
Open-angle glaucoma characteristically causes loss of the nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell layer, as illustrated in the figure. The remaining layers of the retina are normal. These pathologic changes explain the clinical findings of nerve fiber layer atrophy and eventual optic nerve changes. Experimental studies in primates show that the earliest structural changes in the retina with chronic elevation of intraocular pressure (IOP) are seen in the ganglion cell dendritic arbors and then the cell body. Eventually, the nerve axon (nerve fiber layer) degenerates.
Today, optical coherence tomography (OCT) use to observe peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness has been established as a means of detecting and monitoring glaucoma. Recently, spectral-domain OCT (SD- OCT) has been used for quantitative assessment of macular thickness, with special attention to the macular RNFL, ganglion cell layer, and inner plexiform layer. However, whether this provides any advantages over assessment of the peripapillary RNFL is still under discussion.



(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What adverse effect of alpha agonists limits their utility in infants and young children?
pool.rationale: Follicular conjunctivitis is the most common side effect of ocular dosing of alpha agonists, and often precipitates cessation of the therapy. Granulomatous uveitis is a very rare side effect. Xerostomia and lethargy are sometimes reported in adults, especially in the elderly. Central nervous system (CNS) depression including apnea, bradycardia, and systemic hypotension are life-threatening side effects that can be seen in infants and young children using topical alpha agonists.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man is on maximum tolerated medical therapy for primary open-angle glaucoma. Vision is 20/25, the intraocular pressure (IOP) in his right eye is 27 mm Hg, the C:D ratio is 0.95 with superior and inferior notches, and there is visual field progression. What is the most appropriate therapeutic intervention at this point?
pool.rationale:
This patient has advanced glaucoma with high IOP, and there is ongoing optic nerve damage, as evidenced by visual field progression. The most appropriate intervention in this patient is trabeculectomy, in order to lower IOP sufficiently and halt or slow down disease progression.
Laser trabeculoplasty, which is expected to lower IOP by 20%-25%, is unlikely to provide sufficient IOP reduction in this patient. In addition, an IOP spike following laser trabeculoplasty may compromise the optic nerve further.
Cyclophotocoagulation is not appropriate in this patient as a first step, because the extent of treatment required to achieve low IOP is likely to result in vision-threatening complications such as macular edema, prolonged hypotony, and phthisis.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of ocular hypotensive prostaglandin analogues?
pool.rationale: Prostaglandin analogues (eg, latanoprost) lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow and decreasing outflow resistance. Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, dorzolamide), beta blockers (eg, timolol), and alpha-2 agonists (eg, brimonidine) decrease aqueous humor production. Parasympathomimetic agents (eg, pilocarpine) and Rho kinase inhibitors (eg, netarsudil) increase trabecular outflow. Hyperosmotic agents (eg, mannitol) increase blood osmolality, thus creating an osmotic gradient to draw water from the eye.

pool.q: In the assessment of a patient with acute bilateral angle closure and a normal axial length, what additional evaluation is necessary to reach an accurate diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Bilateral angle closure is not common and is especially uncommon in eyes with a normal axial length. The presentation of bilateral angle closure should strongly suggest uveal effusions due to use of a systemic medication, most commonly topiramate.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In pigment dispersion syndrome, what clinical finding would change after peripheral laser iridotomy?
pool.rationale:
Laser iridotomy is indicated for the presence of pupillary block with primary acute angle-closure glaucoma, as well as additional diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Patients with pigmentary dispersion syndrome / pigmentary glaucoma display "reverse pupillary block" configuration, where the iris takes on a posterior bowing appearance. LPI has been shown to relieve posterior or concave bowing of the iris, but multiple studies have failed to show a clear benefit of LPI to treat pigmentary dispersion or pigmentary glaucoma.
The other answer choices (midperipheral iris transillumination, Krukenberg spindle, dense trabecular pigmentation) are all findings associated with pigment dispersion syndrome and are not expected to change significantly after an LPI.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of topical medications should be used with caution for a patient who has both chronic symptomatic trichiasis and glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Prostaglandin analogues, which are used to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) by increasing outflow via the uveoscleral pathway and, to a variable extent, decreasing outflow resistance, are also known to stimulate growth of eyelash follicles. In the setting of chronic symptomatic trichiasis, it may be advisable to avoid this class of medication, because eyelash regrowth may occur more rapidly and worsen the trichiasis.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors may be a cause of chronic epithelial toxicity in some patients, but are not directly related to trichiasis. Alpha-2 agonists have a relatively high rate of allergic complications, but again are not related to trichiasis. Beta blockers should be used with caution in patients with a history of asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

pool.q: What is the rate of aqueous humor formation during sleep compared with the rate during waking hours?

options.d: the same as during waking hours

pool.rationale: During waking hours, the rate of aqueous humor formation is normally about 2–3 μL/min. During sleep, the rate decreases by about 50%. There are no known cases of glaucoma that are caused by overproduction of aqueous humor.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging modality provides an absolute measurement of the retinal nerve fiber layer thickness?

options.d: red free nerve fiber layer photography

pool.rationale:
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) uses low-coherence interferometry to provide high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina. With OCT, quantitative measurements of the entire retinal thickness or the thickness of specific layers can be performed. Thus, OCT provides direct measurement of the RNFL thickness.
With confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (used by the Heidelberg Retinal Tomogram or HRT), RNFL is measured indirectly by measuring the distance between the retinal surface and a reference plane that is 50 microns below it.
Scanning laser polarimetry (used by the GDx device) provides an estimate of the RNFL thickness by measuring the amount of phase retardation of polarized light as it passes through the RNFL; this retardation is proportional to the RNFL thickness.
Red-free NFL photography is a qualitative method to assess the retinal nerve fiber layer.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For 2 days, a patient complains of halos and blurred vision, with mild eye pain in his left eye. His intraocular pressure (IOP) is 14 mm Hg OD and 46 mm Hg OS. There is no conjunctival injection. There are a few inferior keratic precipitates, and the anterior chamber is deep with rare circulating cells. Eight months previously, the patient had a similar episode that resolved within days on eyedrops. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: This patient has characteristic features of glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome). Such patients are often mildly or minimally symptomatic despite markedly elevated IOP. On examination, only a few discrete keratic precipitates may be present. Episodes are usually unilateral and recurrent, with normalization of IOP in between attacks. Although attacks are episodic, patients can develop glaucomatous disc damage and field loss. In cases with progressive damage, a functioning filtering bleb can prevent the acute IOP elevations associated with attacks. Unlike glaucomatocyclitic crisis, herpetic uveitis is generally associated with more inflammation and discomfort. Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is more insidious without episodic attacks of elevated IOP. Angle-closure glaucoma is associated with pain and a shallow chamber.

pool.q: A 58-year-old patient with a history of below-knee amputation underwent a vitrectomy with endolaser 3 years prior for a tractional retinal detachment. He presents to the emergency resident clinic with elevated IOP of 68 mm Hg, severe pain, and decreased vision in the previously operated eye. The patient has a narrow anterior chamber peripherally and centrally, without iris bombé. Topical drops in the office do not lower the intraocular tensions significantly, and an emergent laser peripheral iridotomy does not alleviate the elevation of pressure, pain, or blurry vision. A medication is given to the patient and it significantly lowers the eye pressure over 30-60 minutes after administration. Although the patient's vision and eye pressure are improving, he suddenly develops confusion, abdominal pain, and a fruity scent to his breath. What medication was given to the patient to bring the intraocular tension down?
pool.rationale:
The patient in the scenario is experiencing malignant glaucoma with acute elevation of intraocular tension, and characteristic shallowing of the anterior chamber in the center and in the periphery. It is believed that the aqueous is misdirected in the posterior chamber, causing anterior rotation of the ciliary body and lens complex, and is not alleviated by peripheral iridotomy or dilation. In cases of acute elevation of IOP intractable to topical medical management, hyperosmotic agents can be used to control the IOP in these patients.
Glycerol is metabolized into sugar and ketone bodies, precipitating hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis in diabetic patients. Systemic hyperosmotic agents, including oral glycerol and intravenous mannitol, create an osmotic gradient between the blood and the vitreous humor, directly drawing water out of the vitreous cavity and decreasing the IOP. The larger the dose, the more rapid the effect.
Other adverse effects of hyperosmotic agents include headache, confusion, back ache, acute congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, and subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhages. Hyperosmotic agents are contraindicated in patients with renal failure or those on dialysis, unlike carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide and neptazane), which can be used with caution.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In phacolytic glaucoma, what cell type contributes to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)?
pool.rationale:
Phacolytic glaucoma occurs when an advanced cataract degenerates to the point where soluble lens proteins pass through the intact lens capsule and are phagocytized by macrophages that accumulate within the anterior chamber (figures). As the lens ages, its protein composition alters with more high-molecular-weight proteins. These proteins can pass through pores in the lens capsule. Macrophages in the anterior chamber become swollen with the lens material and can be demonstrated in anterior chamber aspirates, filled with numerous cytoplasmic vacuoles. The macrophages block the trabecular meshwork, leading to elevated IOP and inflammation. The macrophages can be seen in the anterior chamber as refractile cells, associated with aqueous flare from the proteinaceous lens material. Keratic precipitates are usually absent. A mature or hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract is present, often with a wrinkled anterior capsule. Lens proteins may precipitate in the chamber angle. Therapy initially is directed to lowering the pressure, but definitive treatment requires cataract extraction and washing out of the anterior chamber.


(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What is the definition of a cyclodialysis?

options.a: a tear of the ciliary body between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibers
options.b: a separation of the ciliary body from the scleral spur
options.c: an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the suprachoroidal space
options.d: a localized separation or tearing away of the iris from its attachment to the ciliary body

pool.rationale: A cyclodialysis cleft is defined as a separation of the ciliary body from the scleral spur, allowing direct access of the aqueous to the suprachoroidal space. The other answers define angle recession (a tear of the ciliary body between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibers), choroidal effusion (an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the suprachoroidal space), and iridodialysis (a localized separation or tearing away of the iris from its attachment to the ciliary body).

pool.q: A 3-month-old infant is found to have Haab striae and high intraocular pressure (IOP). What IOP-lowering treatment should be avoided?
pool.rationale: Congenital or infantile glaucoma is considered a surgical disease because long-term medication use in young children can be associated with significant side effects. Goniotomy or trabeculotomy are the first-line surgical options for congenital glaucoma. Medications can be used to temporize until surgical therapy can be performed. Topical or systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can be used while monitoring for side effects; however, brimonidine is contraindicated in infants and young children because of possible central nervous system depression and apnea.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What percentage of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) cases in the US are caused by myocilin gene mutations?
pool.rationale: GLC1A, also referred to as TIGR/MYOC, was the first gene described for POAG. Myocilin mutations are present in 4% of the general POAG population. In contrast, up to 33% of juvenile open-angle glaucoma pedigrees harbor myocilin mutations.

pool.q: Which parameter of the modified Goldmann equation cannot be directly measured clinically and must be calculated from the other parameters of the equation?
pool.rationale: Outflow facility is measured with tonography, aqueous humor formation rate with fluorophotometry, and episcleral venous pressure with venomanometry. All these procedures are noninvasive. In contrast, direct measurement of uveoscleral flow rate is an invasive process that involves perfusion of a tracer into the anterior segment of the eye followed by estimation of the tissue distribution of the tracer. Thus uveoscleral outflow rate must be calculated by using the Goldmann equation and the parameters intraocular pressure (IOP), aqueous humor flow rate, outflow facility, and episcleral venous pressure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What systemic disease, aside from connective tissue disorders, predisposes a person to a steroid-induced intraocular pressure (IOP) rise?
pool.rationale: Systemic diseases that increase the risk of a corticosteroid-related IOP rise include connective tissue disorders and type 1 diabetes. Other risk factors for steroid-related IOP rise include a history of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), a first-degree relative with POAG, very young age (<6 years) or older age, and myopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred time for intraocular pressure (IOP) measurement when performing examination under anesthesia?

options.b: 15 minutes after induction of general anesthesia
options.c: immediately after induction of general anesthesia

pool.rationale: General anesthesia is usually required to measure IOP in older infants and young children. However, most general anesthetics profoundly lower IOP, with the exception of chloral hydrate, which does not affect IOP, and ketamine, which increases IOP. Endotracheal intubation and induced laryngospasm can increase IOP. To minimize the effect of these variables, the preferred time for IOP measurement is immediately after induction of general anesthesia and before intubation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with chronic angle-closure glaucoma develops a shallow chamber 3 days after trabeculectomy. On examination, he has a low bleb, a patent surgical iridectomy, no choroidal effusions, and an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 15 mm Hg. What is the best initial treatment option?

options.b: injection of viscoelastic material into the anterior chamber

pool.rationale:
When the anterior chamber shallows postoperatively in the absence of overfiltration or choroidal effusions, one must have a high index of suspicion for aqueous misdirection. This rare condition is seen most often after trabeculectomy done for angle-closure glaucoma. Patients in aqueous misdirection will often have elevated IOP; however, the pressure can be "normal" with a functioning filtering surgery.
Cycloplegic therapy should be initiated in an attempt to normalize the anatomy. Reformation of the anterior chamber is avoided, as the increased posterior pressure will prevent this treatment from being effective. A bandage contact lens is useful in treating a bleb leak, but with a bleb leak the intraocular pressure will invariably be low in the early postoperative period. Steroids are often increased in the setting of hypotony/choroidal effusions to decrease inflammation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What layer of the optic nerve can be better visualized with the ophthalmoscope using the red-free (green) filter?
pool.rationale: This is a useful finding to know in normal optic nerve appearance. Axons in the nerve fiber layer of the normal eye may best be seen with red-free illumination. The nerve fibers travel as bundles of axons from the peripheral retina to converge at the optic nerve head and look like fine striations. This is the layer that atrophies in glaucoma and thus one can see a reduction in the nerve fiber layer brightness (either focally or diffusely) in a glaucoma patient with thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL). Normally, the brightness and striations are more easily seen in the superior and inferior poles as compared to the temporal and nasal regions. When there is RNFL loss, the difference in brightness between the vertical and horizontal regions decreases. Try to appreciate the NFL with the green filter in normal patients and glaucoma patients. The more normals one sees, the better one can appreciate abnormal findings.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A concave peripheral iris is commonly found in what type of glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Pigmentary glaucoma has a concave iris configuration thought to be due to reverse pupillary block. The backbowed iris rubs against the zonules, liberating pigment and creating characteristic midperipheral transillumination defects, pigment deposits on the corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle) and elsewhere, and potentially elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) because of pigment clogging the trabecular meshwork.
Plateau iris syndrome has a flat iris approach to a narrow peripheral angle, with a characteristic double hump on indentation gonioscopy.
Aqueous misdirection will present with the iris and lens pushed forward, narrowing and/or closing the angle. The iris does not take on a bombé configuration.
Pseudoexfoliation glaucoma can present with a flat or convex iris due to relative pupillary block from zonular weakness.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old white man presents with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 24 mm Hg OD and 26 mm Hg OS, a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.5 with healthy neuroretinal rims OU, full visual fields and a central corneal thickness (CCT) of 625 microns OU. What would the next most reasonable course of action be?
pool.rationale: This patient has elevated IOP without evidence of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Given the CCT, the measurement will be artifactually elevated due to a thicker than average cornea. In addition, the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study found similar patients with a corneal thickness >588 microns had very low rates of conversion to open-angle glaucoma at 5 years. In this case, observation is the most reasonable option.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Deposition of pseudoexfoliation material in what ocular structure increases the risk of complications associated with cataract extraction?
pool.rationale:
Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is characterized by the deposition of a fibrillar material in the anterior segment of the eye. Deposition on the lens zonules results in zonular fiber weakness, which predisposes affected eyes to zonular dehiscence, vitreous loss, and lens instability during and after cataract surgery.
Deposits on or in the anterior chamber angle, ciliary processes, and the corneal endothelium do not typically have any impact on cataract surgery outcomes. Poor pupillary dilation is common in pseudoexfoliation syndrome, likely due to infiltration of the fibrillar material into the iris stroma, and the surgeon must be familiar with techniques to enlarge the pupil and be vigilant for problems associated with small-pupil cataract surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 2-year-old boy with congenital glaucoma presents for examination. Both corneas are cloudy, and his intraocular pressure (IOP) is 28 mm Hg in both eyes. What procedure would be the most suitable for this patient?
pool.rationale: The correct answer is trabeculotomy. The presence of childhood glaucoma is an indication for surgery. Goniotomy and trabeculotomy are the preferred procedures. Goniotomy is possible only in an eye with a relative clear cornea, whereas trabeculotomy may be performed whether the cornea is clear or cloudy. For an eye that has failed these procedures, there is a debate whether the next step should be trabeculotomy or a glaucoma drainage device.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the stimulus used to test the peripheral visual field in frequency-doubling technology (FDT) perimetry?

options.a: A blue stimulus is projected onto a yellow background.
options.b: A kinetic stimulus is moved from a non-seeing to a seeing area of the visual field.
options.c: A stationary stimulus of varying intensity is presented at predetermined locations to measure threshold.
options.d: A high temporal frequency counter phase flicker stimulus is used.

pool.rationale: FDT perimetry is a visual field testing paradigm that uses low spatial sinusoidal grating undergoing rapid-phase reversal flicker. SITA SWAP (Swedish interactive thresholding algorithm short-wavelength automated perimetry) testing employs a blue light stimulus on a yellow background for early glaucoma detection. Kinetic perimetry involves moving a target from a non-seeing to a seeing area. Static perimetry varies a stationary stimulus at locations and changes the brightness, size, and duration of the stimulus to determine the threshold.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What interventions were compared in the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial?

options.a: medication and laser trabeculoplasty versus observation
options.b: argon laser trabeculoplasty versus selective laser trabeculoplasty

pool.rationale: The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT) evaluated the effect of immediate pressure reduction versus observation on the progression of early glaucoma. Patients with advanced field loss, IOP > 30 mm Hg and visual acuity < 20/40 were excluded. Eligible patients were randomized to treatment with betaxolol plus laser trabeculoplasty or to observation. At 6 years, 45% of treated patients progressed as compared to 62% of untreated patients. Treatment reduced IOP by an average of 25%. The EMGT was the first trial with an adequately powered, untreated control arm that showed treatment delayed progression in glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the effect of applying pressure with a Goldmann-type, large-diameter gonioscopy lens?

options.a: This might help differentiate between appositional and synechial angle closure.
options.b: This might help to break an attack of acute angle-closure glaucoma.
options.c: This might indent the sclera and falsely narrow the angle.
options.d: This might indent the cornea and falsely open the angle.

pool.rationale: Applying pressure with a Goldmann lens results in force at the limbus and anterior sclera, which might falsely narrow the angle. The most common method of slit-lamp iridocorneal angle evaluation is indirect gonioscopy. The main types of indirect gonioscopy lenses are large-diameter lenses, like the 3-mirror Goldmann lens, and smaller-diameter lenses, like the 4-mirror Zeiss or Sussman lenses. Goldmann lenses are vaulted, requiring a coupling agent such as methylcellulose to fill the space between the cornea and lens to visualize the angle. The lens rim diameter is larger than the cornea, so posterior pressure causes indentation of the sclera and not the cornea. This can cause artificial narrowing of the angle and reflux of blood into the Schlemm canal. On the other hand, pressure on smaller-diameter lenses indents the cornea and forces fluid into the angle recess. Unintentional pressure can falsely open the angle, but intentional pressure can allow the examiner to distinguish between appositional and synechial angle closure. Corneal indentation can also help break an attack of angle closure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a relative contraindication to trabeculectomy surgery?
pool.rationale: Incisional surgery is indicated when maximally tolerated medical therapy, including laser trabeculoplasty, is insufficient to prevent progression of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Other indications include poor adherence to prescribed medical therapy. Relative contraindications include any condition that may predispose to conjunctival scarring, including history of prior conjunctival surgery, active anterior segment neovascularization, and active uveitis or scleritis. Other relative contraindications include younger age and African American race.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: After surgery for congenital cataracts, how long should a patient be monitored for the development of glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Glaucoma develops in 15% to 50% of children who have undergone surgery for congenital cataracts. The risk factors for aphakic glaucoma are cataract surgery in the first year of life, small corneal diameters, and postoperative complications. In most cases, aphakic glaucoma develops within 3 years after cataract surgery. However, these patients are always at risk for developing glaucoma and should be monitored lifelong.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What optic disc finding may be more common in normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) than in primary open-angle glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Disc hemorrhages may be more common in NTG than in POAG (but can be seen in both conditions). Further, differences in optic nerve appearance and visual field defects between patients with NTG and those with high-tension POAG are not uniformly confirmed in studies. Therefore, for any individual patient, there is no characteristic abnormality of the optic nerve or visual field that distinguishes NTG from high-tension POAG.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What are the gender and laterality demographic characteristics of primary congenital glaucoma?
pool.rationale: The pathophysiologic defect of primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is increased resistance to outflow through the trabecular meshwork, believed to be secondary to dysgenesis of neural crest cell-derived angle structures. It most commonly affects males (65%) and is usually bilateral (70%). This demographic information is important to consider when differentiating this disease from other possible diagnoses. Of note, those affected by PCG have a 2% chance of having offspring with the disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What optic disc finding is most suggestive of glaucomatous optic neuropathy?
pool.rationale: Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is characterized by progressive cupping.  Though early glaucomatous changes, such as a generalized enlargement of the cup, can be subtle, more specific changes include vertical cup elongation, rim notching, and cupping to the rim margin.  Less specific signs of glaucoma include exposed lamina cribrosa, nasal vessel displacement, baring of the circumlinear blood vessels, and beta zone peripapillary atrophy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Fuchs uveitis syndrome (formerly Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis) is associated with a constellation of examination findings. What anterior segment abnormality would lead an ophthalmologist to consider an alternative diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Fuchs uveitis syndrome is a chronic form of uveitis (or iridocyclitis) characterized by iris heterochromia, low-grade anterior chamber reaction, stellate keratic precipitate, posterior subcapsular cataract, and secondary open-angle glaucoma. On gonioscopy, fine vessels crossing the trabecular meshwork may be seen, but unlike neovascularization, they are not accompanied by a fibrous membrane and do not usually cause peripheral anterior synechiae or angle closure. These vessels are fragile and may bleed spontaneously or during surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What topical medication can help relieve pupillary block caused by microspherophakia?
pool.rationale: In microspherophakia, the lens has a spherical or globular shape that can lead to pupillary block and acute angle closure. Miotics such as pilocarpine can worsen the condition by rotating the ciliary body forward and loosening the zonules, allowing the lens to become more globular. Cycloplegics such as atropine can tighten the zonules, flatten the lens, and pull it posteriorly, breaking the pupillary block. Phenylephrine dilates the pupil but does not have cycloplegic action. Apraclonidine is an alpha-2 agonist used in intraocular pressure reduction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How does pilocarpine reduce intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale:
Pilocarpine is a direct-acting parasympathomimetic agent that contracts the longitudinal ciliary muscle fibers that insert into the scleral spur and trabecular meshwork. This increases outflow of aqueous via the trabecular meshwork.
Nowadays, because of its side effects and the need for dosing 3 to 4 times a day, it is infrequently prescribed for long-term use. Side effects include induced myopia and difficulty seeing in dim light, due to miosis. It may also be associated with paradoxical angle closure (due to forward shift of the lens-iris diaphragm), retinal detachment, and breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What contact tonometer can be used without a corneal anesthetic?
pool.rationale:
A rebound tonometer rapidly and painlessly contacts the cornea to measure intraocular pressure (IOP) without the need for anesthetic. This tonometer has been used widely in the pediatric population.
The pneumotonometer and dynamic contour tonometer (DCT) are both contact methods requiring prolonged corneal contact, necessitating anesthetic. The DCT is less affected by corneal biomechanics, making it useful in postrefractive surgical eyes.
The ocular response analyzer is a noncontact method. Since there is no corneal contact, no anesthetic is required. The tonometer uses several air puffs to measure IOP and corneal hysteresis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the procedure of choice in treating medically uncontrolled neovascular glaucoma (NVG) when the patient has good visual potential?
pool.rationale: NVG is often very difficult to control medically. The success rate of trabeculectomy is very poor in managing NVG. In a patient with good visual potential, a primary tube shunt is indicated, ideally after anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatment with or without panretinal photocoagulation. If the patient has poor visual potential, cyclophotocoagulation is an appropriate alternative. Goniosynechialysis can lead to bleeding and worsen IOP control.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What laser wavelength is most commonly used for transscleral cyclophotocoagulation?
pool.rationale:
Cyclophotocoagulation is most commonly performed with the 810-nm diode laser, which has replaced the 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser as well as cryotherapy for ciliary body ablation.
The 514-nm argon and 647-nm krypton lasers are not used for cyclophotocoagulation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: By what mechanism does pilocarpine reduce intraocular pressure?

options.a: by direct stimulation of muscarinic receptors, resulting in contraction of the ciliary muscle and increased trabecular outflow
options.b: by contraction of the ciliary muscle, resulting in an increased uveoscleral outflow
options.c: by inhibition of acetylcholinesterase and prolonged effect of natural acetylcholine, causing ciliary muscle contraction and increased trabecular outflow
options.d: by inhibition of carbonic anhydrase, causing a decreased rate of aqueous production.

pool.rationale: Parasympathomimetics cause contraction of the ciliary muscle, tightening of the scleral spur, and tension on the trabecular beams, leading to increased trabecular outflow. Direct-acting agents, such as pilocarpine, directly stimulate the muscarinic receptors at the motor end plates. Indirect agents, such as echothiophate iodine, inhibit acetylcholinesterase and prolong the effect of natural acetylcholine at the motor end plates. Carbachol has a mixed direct and indirect mechanism.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of laser surgery is most useful in the management of neovascular glaucoma due to a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)?
pool.rationale:
Neovascular glaucoma (NVG) is a type of secondary angle-closure glaucoma characterized by fibrovascular proliferation in the anterior chamber angle and the iris. The most common causes are diabetic retinopathy and central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO).
Panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) is the initial laser treatment of choice to treat retinal ischemia and eliminate the stimulus for angiogenesis. Depending on the extent of synechial angle closure, PRP may or may not normalize IOP.
Diode laser cyclophotocoagulation is indicated for IOP control when the visual potential is poor (less than 20/400) and maximum medical therapy is ineffective. However, cyclodestruction does not address the underlying mechanism for neovascularization and cannot replace PRP.
Focal macular photocoagulation is used for the treatment of macular edema (ME), but it is not effective for ME in this case, due to the CRVO.
Goniophotocoagulation refers to direct laser treatment of new vessels in the angle and is not indicated, because neovascularization in the anterior segment regresses with the treatment of retinal ischemia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What corneal characteristics increase the risk of development of glaucoma in patients who are glaucoma suspects?

options.a: low central corneal thickness (CCT) and high corneal hysteresis
options.b: high central corneal thickness (CCT) and high corneal hysteresis
options.c: low central corneal thickness (CCT) and low corneal hysteresis
options.d: high central corneal thickness (CCT) and low corneal hysteresis

pool.rationale:
Corneal hysteresis is the difference between IOP measured during the initial corneal indentation and IOP measured during corneal rebound. Reduced (low) corneal hysteresis is associated with an increased risk of developing visual field defects in glaucoma suspects and with disease progression in patients with confirmed glaucoma.
Thicker corneas resist deformation during tonometry, which results in an overestimation of IOP, while thinner corneas may give an artificially low IOP reading. Additionally, a thin central cornea may be a biomarker for another risk factor independent of IOP measurement.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the mechanism by which topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitor therapy decreases intraocular pressure?

options.a: increased aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork
options.c: creation of an osmotic gradient to reduce intraocular fluid volume
options.d: increased aqueous humor outflow via the uveoscleral pathway

pool.rationale: Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, dorzolamide) decrease aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium, thus decreasing intraocular pressure. Parasympathomimetic agents (eg, pilocarpine) and Rho kinase inhibitors (eg, netarsudil) increase trabecular outflow. Prostaglandin analogues (eg, latanoprost) increase uveoscleral outflow. Hyperosmotic agents (eg, mannitol) increase blood osmolality, thus creating an osmotic gradient to draw water from the eye.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 36-year-old woman develops unilateral decreased vision and a change in the shape of her pupil. Her IOP is 36 mm Hg and her endothelium has a beaten-bronze appearance. Following initiation of maximal topical ocular antihypertensive medications, her IOP remains 31 mm Hg. What is the next recommended step in managing this patient's condition?
pool.rationale:
This patient has iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome, and the best next step is incisional surgery, such as anterior chamber tube shunt placement. ICE syndrome is a unilateral, acquired abnormality of the corneal endothelium, usually affecting women between 20 and 50 years of age. Glaucoma in ICE syndrome is caused by migration of abnormal endothelial cells over the trabecular meshwork. Contraction of this membrane can cause characteristic high peripheral anterior synechiae and secondary angle closure.
Because there is no element of pupillary block, iridotomy would not be helpful. Angle procedures such as iridoplasty and trabeculoplasty do not relieve elevated IOP due to the angle abnormalities. These patients require surgical bypass of angle obstruction if medication fails to control IOP. Trabeculectomy or glaucoma tube-shunt implantation are reasonable surgical options; however, even filtering surgery may be less successful in these patients due to late endothelialization of the fistula in trabeculectomies.

pool.q: What commercially available topical beta-blocker is a selective ß-1 antagonist?

pool.q: What is the reason to avoid the 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock positions on the eye when performing transscleral diode cyclophotocoagulation (CPC)?

options.b: There is greater risk of sympathetic ophthalmia of the fellow eye when treatment is applied at this location.
options.c: There is greater pigmentation of the eye at this location.
options.d: The ciliary nerves generally enter the eye at this location.

pool.q: In addition to the presence of cataract, clinical features of phacomorphic glaucoma include what feature?
pool.rationale:
Phacomorphic glaucoma is characterized by anterior chamber shallowing from an enlarged (or enlarging) lens. Although anterior chamber cell and flare, vitreous inflammation, and iris neovascularization can complicate late disease, they are not a required component for diagnosis.
As the lens thickens in the anterior–posterior dimension it can cause pupillary block and induce secondary angle-closure glaucoma, or it can physically push the iris forward and thus cause shallowing of the anterior chamber. Often, the patient presents with a red, painful eye and a history of vision changes as a result of cataract formation prior to the acute event. The cornea may be edematous, and gonioscopy reveals a closed anterior chamber angle. Initial management includes medical treatment to lower the IOP. The condition may respond to laser iridotomy, but definitive treatment consists of cataract extraction.
Phacomorphic narrowing of the angle generally occurs slowly with formation of the cataract.

pool.q: The highest prevalence of acute primary angle closure is reported in populations of what racial or ethnic group?

0.1% - 0.4% in populations of European ancestry
0.1% - 0.6% in African populations
2.5% - 4.8% in the Inuit populations > 40 years in Alaska and Greenland (the highest known prevalence; 20 to 40 times higher than in the white population)
0.4% - 1.4% in East Asian populations
1.5% in the population 50 years old and older in Guangzhou, China

pool.q: What type of perimetry may be used to detect glaucomatous visual field loss earlier than conventional white-on-white perimetry?
pool.rationale:
Frequency-doubling technology (FDT), flicker-defined form (FDF), and short-wavelength automated perimetry (SWAP) all target subpopulations of retinal ganglion cells by evaluating specific aspects of visual function. FDT perimetry selectively evaluates the M pathway, and longitudinal studies have shown that abnormalities on FDT may precede detectable SAP changes in many patients. FDF also may stimulate the M cell pathway, and there is emerging evidence that it may be useful for early glaucoma diagnosis. SWAP does not appear to have better diagnostic ability than standard automated perimetry and is being utilized less in clinical practice.
Goldmann kinetic perimetry is a manual perimetric technique that is not suitable for detection of subtle changes in visual field. It can sometimes be more useful in patients unable to complete automated static perimetry, as technicians can keep patients more engaged and attentive during this type of testing.
Confrontation visual field testing cannot detect early glaucomatous defects, only gross deficits.
Visual evoked cortical potential testing may be used in assessing retinal and optic nerve disorders, but it is not utilized commonly in most clinical settings for measurement of glaucomatous visual field loss.

pool.q: According to the Goldmann equation, what is the ratio of increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) to the increase in episcleral venous pressure in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg)?
pool.rationale:
According to the Goldmann equation, where Po = (F - U)/C + Pv where Po is the IOP in mm Hg, F is the rate of aqueous formation, U is the rate of aqueous humor drainage through the pressure-insensitive uveoscleral pathway in microliters per minute (μL/min), C is the facility of outflow through the pressure-sensitive trabecular pathway in microliters per minute per mm Hg (μL/min/mm Hg ) and Pv is the episcleral venous pressure in mm Hg, the IOP rises 1 mm Hg for every 1 mm Hg of rise in episcleral venous pressure.
Patients with Sturge-Weber, carotid-cavernous sinus fistulas, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and thyroid eye disease (partial increase) have increased episcleral venous pressure from obstruction of venous return to the heart or from shunting of blood from the arterial to the venous system. Episcleral venous pressure is normally relatively stable, ranging from 6 mm Hg to 9 mm Hg measured with special equipment. Increased episcleral venous pressure can increase outflow resistance by collapsing the Schlemm canal and may alter uveoscleral outflow.

pool.q: In the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), what risk factor predicted who might develop glaucoma?

In this study, increased risk of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) was associated with decrease in central corneal thickness (CCT), and increased age, vertical and horizontal cup-to-disc ratio, pattern standard deviation, and baseline intraocular pressure (IOP).

pool.q: What is an advantage of fixed-combination drops in lowering intraocular pressure?

options.a: Fixed combinations have enhanced efficacy due to a synergistic effect, compared with the efficacy of their individual components.
options.b: Fixed combinations are all preservative free.
options.c: Fixed combinations improve patient adherence and therefore long-term prognosis.
options.d: Fixed combinations have fewer ocular side effects than their individual components.

pool.rationale: Fixed combinations improve patient adherence and therefore long-term prognosis. Although fixed-combination drops reduce the exposure to the preservative BAC compared with using several individual medication drops, preparations are not preservative free unless specifically formulated. The efficacy of the fixed combination is generally greater than each of its individual components; however, it is not greater than use of both drops separately. In fact, using the unfixed combination generally provides a slightly (statistically nonsignificant) greater reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) than the fixed combination containing the same medicines. The side effects of fixed-combination drops are the same as for both drugs given individually.

pool.q: A 21-year-old man with a history of blunt trauma and uncomplicated hyphema of the right eye 1 month ago presents with a red, painful right eye and blurred vision that started 4 hours ago. He is in pupillary block with an intraocular pressure of 50 mm Hg. Despite corneal edema, you can see that his lens is clear. What is the most likely cause of his acute condition?
pool.rationale:
Forward displacement of the lens can cause pupillary block and result in iris bombé, angle closure, and acute rise in intraocular pressure. This patient's history of recent blunt injury, which was significant enough to cause a hyphema, suggests traumatic zonular laxity and excess forward motion of the lens (ie, a form of ectopia lentis) as the cause of his pupillary block.
Phacomorphic glaucoma can cause both chronic and acute angle closure, often with a component of pupillary block, but is unlikely in this young patient with a visibly clear lens. Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is a well-established cause of zonular weakness, anterior movement of the lens-iris interface, and subluxation of the crystalline lens. However, pseudoexfoliation syndrome is strongly age-related and rarely seen in patients under 50 years old.
Angle recession is common following blunt ocular trauma. Intraocular pressure elevation due to recession can occur immediately following the trauma or months to years later. It does not, however, result in pupillary block, which was present in this patient.

pool.q: What reliability index can be high in automated static perimetry, although the test still may be considered accurate?
pool.rationale:
Reliability indices help in evaluating test reliability and include false positive errors, false negative errors, and fixation loss rate. Test duration is not considered a reliability index but can be used to judge patient response time to stimuli.
The false-positive rate measures the patient's tendency to press the response button when there is no stimulus (ie, "trigger happy"). Higher than 15% indicates an unreliable test. False-negative rates measure the tendency of the patient to not respond even when visible stimulus is presented. This could indicate inattentiveness of the patient, but may also be seen with increased variability in areas of damage; therefore, high false-negative rates should not necessarily result in throwing out of test results. Fixation losses occur when the patient looks away from the central target ("chasing the lights") and can result in unreliable fields and inability to accurately map the physiologic blind spot.

pool.q: A 60-year-old woman with history of primary angle-closure glaucoma, status post successful laser peripheral iridotomy in the past, has uncontrolled intraocular pressure (IOP) on medical treatment. The visual acuity is 20/25, there is synechial angle closure for 270 degrees, and the cup-to-disc (C:D) ratio is 0.9. What is the most appropriate intervention for this patient?
pool.rationale:
Glaucoma filtration surgery is indicated for IOP lowering in this patient with extensive synechial angle closure and advanced cupping of the optic nerve.
Iridotomy will not alter angle anatomy or lower IOP in the presence of extensive synechial closure and is not indicated.
Trabeculoplasty is potentially feasible in only 90 degrees of the angle and would not likely provide adequate IOP lowering with such a small area of treatment.
Cyclophotocoagulation can be employed for IOP control in refractory glaucoma but is not indicated as the first surgical intervention in this patient.

pool.q: Following successful goniotomy for elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) due to primary congenital glaucoma (PCG), what is the most common reason for poor visual outcome?
pool.rationale:
Amblyopia is a common cause of visual compromise, particularly in patients with unilateral glaucoma, corneal opacification, and/or anisometropia. The clinician should treat amblyopia aggressively, addressing conditions contributing to its development, such as refractive error, strabismus, cataract, and corneal clouding. Elevated IOP can lead to buphthalmos in patients with PCG and to progressive myopia and anisometropia in patients with juvenile open-angle glaucoma (JOAG). Haab striae and corneal scarring may cause astigmatism. Refractive errors should be corrected with spectacles, and use of protective eyewear should be encouraged.
It is imperative that pediatric glaucoma patients are monitored for amblyopia and treated appropriately to increase the likelihood of good visual outcomes. Retinal detachment, cataract, and endophthalmitis are uncommon after goniotomy.

pool.q: What corneal abnormality is commonly seen in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome?
pool.rationale: Posterior embryotoxon (visible in an anterior segment examination) is a prominent and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line that is characteristic for Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. Adhesions from the cornea to Schwalbe line can vary from threadlike and thin to broad bands of iris tissue. The remainder of the cornea in patients with this condition is otherwise normal.

pool.q: What condition is associated with a higher risk of developing aqueous misdirection following trabeculectomy?
pool.rationale: Patients with prior acute or chronic angle closure are at highest risk for aqueous misdirection following trabeculectomy. Patients with deep anterior chambers preoperatively, which would be expected in the other listed conditions (juvenile open-angle glaucoma, angle recession, and pigment dispersion), are at lower risk for aqueous misdirection.

pool.q: Based on the results of clinical trial data from the OHTS (Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study), what clinical finding, aside from high intraocular pressure (IOP), has been found to be a risk factor for progression of glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Data from clinical trials have found that a number of risk factors are associated with the progression of primary open-angle glaucoma. These include elevated IOP, reduced perfusion pressure, advanced age, positive family history, thin central cornea, and race. Thin central cornea was noted in the OHTS and the European Glaucoma Prevention Study (EGPS). The role of various systemic factors (eg, diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis) has been debated, and available data are inconclusive. Presence of disc hemorrhage was found to be a risk factor for glaucomatous progression in the Collaborative Normal-Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS) and the Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT).

pool.q: What is the defining abnormality seen in eyes with angle-recession glaucoma?

options.a: a tear in the ciliary body muscle

pool.rationale: Traumatic recession of the anterior chamber angle is due to a tear in the ciliary body between the longitudinal and circular muscles, but only when there is concurrent damage to the meshwork does angle recession possibly lead to glaucoma. Iridodialysis is a rupture of the iris at the thinnest portion of the diaphragm, which does not cause glaucoma. Similarly, lens subluxation alone (without hemorrhage) does not cause glaucoma.

pool.q: A patient with high myopia is at increased risk of what type of glaucoma?
pool.rationale: A patient with high myopia is at increased risk of primary open-angle glaucoma. Pigment dispersion syndrome is more common in moderately myopic eyes. Angle-closure glaucoma is associated with hyperopia. Pseudoexfoliation is not associated with a particular refractive error.

pool.q: What form of secondary glaucoma is associated with higher rates of vitreous loss during cataract extraction?
pool.rationale: Cataract extraction in the setting of pseudoexfoliation syndrome is more challenging and carries a higher rate of vitreous loss. Pupils often dilate poorly, making lens visualization more difficult without pupil stretching. In addition, poor zonular support can make removal and placement of an IOL more difficult. Postoperatively, there is a higher rate of capsular phimosis in these eyes. While pigment dispersion syndrome, steroid-induced glaucoma, and plateau iris syndrome do not predispose to vitreous loss, they are associated with selected other cataract surgery complications. For instance, one should be cognizant of protecting the cornea in the setting of a shallow chamber associated with plateau iris and reducing irrigation to prevent overdeepening of the anterior chamber in a myopic eye with pigment dispersion.

pool.q: What anterior chamber depth predisposes an eye to primary angle closure?
pool.rationale: An anterior chamber depth of less than 2.5 mm predisposes an eye to primary angle closure. The anterior chamber depth varies from 1.5 mm to 4.0 mm, with an average value of 3.0 mm. The most important risk factors predisposing an eye for angle-closure glaucoma are shallow anterior chamber, thick lens, increased anterior curvature of the lens, short axial length, and small corneal diameter and radius of curvature. Other risk factors include female sex, increasing age, Asian or Inuit ancestry, and a first-degree relative with angle closure.

pool.q: In Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), what was identified as an important risk factor for the development of glaucoma in patients with ocular hypertension?
pool.rationale: The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study was the first trial to prospectively document that thinner central corneal thickness was a risk factor for the development of glaucoma. In multivariate analysis, thinner central corneal thickness (CCT) emerged as a risk factor regardless of age, baseline IOP, or cup-disc ratio. This study underscored the importance of assessing CCT in all patients with ocular hypertension. Myopia, diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease were not associated with conversion to glaucoma.

pool.q: How does intravenous mannitol reduce intraocular pressure (IOP)?
pool.rationale:
Hyperosmotic agents, which include intravenous mannitol and oral glycerol, are used to control acute IOP elevations. Intravenous mannitol increases blood osmolality, causing an osmotic gradient between the blood and the vitreous humor; this gradient draws water from the vitreous cavity and reduces IOP. The larger the dose and the more rapid the administration, the greater the IOP reduction. The effect of hyperosmotic agents is transient because of rapid equilibration of the osmotic gradient.
Side effects include headache, confusion, acute congestive heart failure, and myocardial infarction. Glycerol can cause hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis in diabetics. Hyperosmotic agents are contraindicated in patients with renal failure.

pool.q: Prospective trials have found several risk factors for the development or progression of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG). In these studies, what factor is associated with progression in POAG?
pool.rationale: In prospective trials, decreased ocular perfusion pressure, thinner cornea, and increasing age have been shown to be important risk factors for progression of glaucoma. Intracranial pressure might have an effect on the translaminar pressure gradient, but has not been studied in clinical trials. Furthermore, lower intracranial pressure has been implicated as a factor in low-tension glaucoma, but has not been explored in a longitudinal trial.

pool.q: What type of lens allows the examiner to perform indentation gonioscopy?
pool.rationale: Indentation gonioscopy requires a gonioprism with a smaller posterior diameter than the corneal diameter. Commonly used lenses include the Zeiss, Posner, and Sussman 4-mirror lenses. A Goldmann 3-mirror lens has a larger diameter. Pressure from this lens can cause reflux of blood into the Schlemm canal. A Koeppe lens is a large diameter direct gonioscopy lens often used intraoperatively. A Hoskins lens is used for laser suture lysis post trabeculectomy.

pool.q: An 18-year-old man underwent an uncomplicated refractive surgery in both eyes for myopia. Since the surgery, he is experiencing glare and halos at night. What topical treatment could improve his symptoms, but also has an increased risk of retinal detachment?
pool.rationale:
Pilocarpine 1% causes miosis, which may reduce postoperative halo/glare but has the adverse complication of increased risk of retinal detachment, especially in myopic patients, possibly by vitreoretinal traction secondary to ciliary muscle contraction, leading to retinal breaks. A thorough dilated examination is recommended prior to prescription of pilocarpine. Pilocarpine is a parasympathomimetic or cholinergic agent that directly stimulates cholinergic receptors on the iris sphincter muscle, causing the muscle to contract and produce miosis. Pilocarpine causes induced myopia by contraction of the ciliary muscle, which takes tension off the zonules, resulting in increased axial lens diameter. Pilocarpine may have a cataractogenic effect. In addition, ciliary muscle spasm may cause brow ache, which usually improves with a few weeks of continued therapy. Atropine, even at a low dose, causes pupillary dilation, which would not be expected to reduce symptoms of glare.
Artificial tears are used to treat dry eye, which may cause glare, but artificial tears are not associated with an increased risk for retinal detachment. Brimonidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, reduces pupillary dilation, which may improve symptoms of glare, but it is not associated with retinal detachment risk.  Brimonidine should not be used in infants and children, due to the risk of central nervous system (CNS) depression, apnea, bradycardia, and hypotension.

pool.q: A 3-year-old child presents with intraocular pressure (IOP) at 28 mm Hg on topical dorzolamide-timolol twice a day and latanoprost at night. On examination, the anterior segment is cloudy, with a corneal diameter measuring 12.5 mm. A cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 is noted with an otherwise normal dilated posterior segment examination. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
pool.rationale:
Definitive treatment for most cases of primary congenital glaucoma is surgical. With a clear cornea, goniotomy and ab externo trabeculotomy are both appropriate options. With a cloudy cornea, ab externo trabeculotomy is the preferred choice. Alpha-2 agonist treatment is contraindicated in children, secondary to the risk of CNS depression. Both trabeculotomy and goniotomy yield a 70%-80% success rate in children between the ages of 3 and 12 months of age.
Cyclodestructive procedures decrease the IOP by means of decreased production of aqueous from ciliary body atrophy. Endocyclophotocoagulation (ECP) has fewer complications than cryotherapy, but both present difficulty in titrating results. Serious potential complications that can occur with cyclodestructive procedures include hypotony, uveitis, retinal detachment, phthisis bulbi, and blindness.

pool.q: What retinal cell type is the primary site of damage in glaucomatous optic neuropathy?
pool.rationale:
Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is progressive degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and their axons, extending from the optic nerve to the major visual centers in the brain (lateral geniculate nucleus). Contributors to retinal ganglion cell death may include direct compression of axonal fibers with distortion of the lamina cribrosa plates and disruption of axoplasmic flow, decreased optic nerve head perfusion, and/or disturbance of vascular autoregulation.
In patients with glaucoma, the intraocular pressure (IOP) at baseline—regardless of its actual level—is too high for retinal ganglion cell function and survival. It has been shown that in most patients with glaucoma, lowering the IOP will stop or slow visual field loss.
