pool.q: An 80-year-old patient has had poor vision in her right eye for at least 10 years. She had sudden pain and redness this morning, with a further drop in her vision. She has very high intraocular pressure (IOP) with corneal edema, cell and flare without keratic precipitates, and an open angle. What type of cataract would this patient be likely to have?
pool.rationale: A morgagnian cataract is a mature cataract in which the cortex becomes liquefied, allowing free movement of the hypermature nucleus within the capsular bag. The liquefied lens particles can leak through the intact lens capsule, causing increased intraocular pressure (IOP); this is called phacolytic glaucoma. Wilson disease is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism  that can lead to development of a sunflower cataract. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition that can lead to development of polychromatic iridescent crystals in the lens cortex called a Christmas-tree cataract. Anterior lenticonus is a localized, cone-shaped deformation of the anterior lens surface that can be associated with Alport syndrome.

pool.q: What factor is associated with increased risk of blindness in primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)?

options.a: high IOP at the time of diagnosis
options.c: visual field loss at the time of diagnosis

pool.rationale: Patients at greatest risk of blindness are those with visual field loss at the time of diagnosis. Elevated IOP and thin cornea are risk factors for the development of POAG. Blindness from glaucoma is 4 times higher in African Americans than in whites.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of iris color change with topical prostaglandin analogue use?

pool.q: What gene has been associated with juvenile open-angle glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
TIGR/MYOC

GLC1A, the first gene linked to open-angle glaucoma, is associated with a subset of juvenile-onset glaucoma. This gene is synonymously referred to as TIGR (trabecular meshwork inducible glucocorticoid response)/MYOC (myocilin) and is associated with 3% of adult-onset, primary open-angle glaucoma cases. Most cases of juvenile open-angle glaucoma have an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, but sporadic cases occasionally occur. Juvenile open-angle glaucoma has been linked to mutations in the TIGR/MYOC gene at the GLC1A locus.

pool.q: A 36-year-old myopic patient has an IOP of 16 mm Hg OD and 28 mm Hg OS. He describes episodic blurry vision and colored halos in his left eye after playing basketball. What finding might be expected on further examination?
pool.rationale: The patient has a characteristic history for pigment dispersion syndrome (PDS), which can result in a Krukenberg spindle on the corneal endothelium. Patients with PDS are typically young, myopic males, and the diagnosis is often made on routine examination. They may notice blurry vision, headaches, or nausea after jarring exercise due to large releases of pigment, which can cause transiently elevated IOP and corneal edema (resulting in haloes around lights). Classic slit-lamp findings include Krukenberg spindle, midperipheral iris transillumination defects, and heavy pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork. Pigment may also accumulate in the iris furrows and at the lens equator (Scheie stripe). The incorrect answer choices are associated with other secondary glaucomas. A widened ciliary body band is found in angle recession, sector iris atrophy is associated with herpetic disease, and peripupillary transillumination defects are found in pseudoexfoliation syndrome.

pool.q: What is the main advantage of an electroablation device when compared to trabeculectomy?

options.b: There is greater intraocular pressure reduction
options.c: It can be combined with cataract surgery.
options.d: There is less risk of bleeding.

pool.rationale:
Trabectome is a minimally invasive glaucoma procedure in which the inner wall of the Schlemm canal is ablated, thereby enabling increased aqueous outflow through physiological pathways.
The intraocular pressure (IOP)-lowering effect of an electroablation device (eg, Trabectome, NeoMedix Inc, Tustin, CA) is limited by the episcleral venous pressure; therefore, the lowest IOP achievable with this procedure alone is usually in the low- to mid-teens, as opposed to trabeculectomy, in which single-digit IOPs can be achieved.
Hyphema or microhyphema is very common after Trabectome, due to blood reflux into the anterior chamber via the open inner wall of the Schlemm canal.
Both Trabectome and trabeculectomy can be combined with cataract surgery.
Unlike trabeculectomy, Trabectome does not create a bleb. Given the potentially devastating consequences of bleb-related complications, this is a major advantage of minimally invasive angle-based glaucoma surgeries such as the Trabectome and a trabecular microbypass stent (eg, iStent, Glaukos Corp, Laguna Hills, CA).

pool.q: What is the most common cause of glaucoma associated with primary or metastatic tumors of the ciliary body?

options.b: angle closure by rotation of the ciliary body
options.c: deposition of tumor cells and inflammatory cells in the trabecular meshwork
options.d: direct invasion of the anterior chamber angle

pool.rationale: Although all of these events (angle closure by rotation of the ciliary body, deposition of tumor cells and inflammatory cells in the trabecular meshwork, direct invasion of the anterior chamber angle, neovascularization of the angle) can cause glaucoma associated with primary or metastatic tumors of the ciliary body, direct invasion of the anterior chamber angle is the most common cause of glaucoma in this setting.

pool.q: In the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS), a higher baseline intraocular pressure (IOP) increased the relative risk of glaucoma at 5 years by what percentage per 1 mm Hg?
pool.rationale: In the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study, a higher baseline IOP (per 1 mm Hg increase) increased the relative risk of glaucoma development by 10%. Other baseline risk factors included older age (22% increased relative risk per decade) and higher pattern standard deviation on visual field (VF) testing (22% increase in relative risk per 0.2 dB increase). pool.q: What characteristic differentiates epithelial ingrowth from fibrous ingrowth?
pool.rationale:
Both epithelial and fibrous proliferation are rare surgical complications that can lead to secondary glaucoma, although the former is known to be more aggressive and associated with a higher risk of elevated intraocular pressure and glaucomatous change. Epithelial ingrowth presents as a grayish, sheetlike growth on the trabecular meshwork, the iris, the ciliary body, and the posterior surface of the cornea. It consists of nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with an avascular subepithelial connective tissue layer. Argon laser will produce white burns on the epithelial membrane for diagnosis.
Unlike epithelial ingrowth, fibrous ingrowth progresses slowly and is often self-limited. It appears as a thick, gray-white vascular retrocorneal membrane with an irregular border. It is more commonly seen than epithelial ingrowth and can cause peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS), in turn destroying the trabecular meshwork. Medications can be used to treat this type of glaucoma without pupillary block.

pool.q: What color irides are most affected by the increased number of melanosomes resulting from latanoprost usage?
pool.rationale: Prostaglandin analogues (PGAs) reduce the intraocular pressure by increasing the uveoscleral outflow, and are often useful in patients with pigmentary glaucoma. Iris color change results from an increased number of melanosomes in melanocytes, with a risk of up to 33% after 5 years of PGA use. The color change is permanent. Studies of latanoprost indicated 79% of patients with green/brown irides and 85% of patients with yellow/brown irides are affected, compared to only 8% of those with blue irides. Eyelash changes (increase in thickness, count, and pigmentation) may also occur. PGA should be used with caution in all forms of inflammatory glaucoma, due to a possible inflammatory response. Patients who have had recurrent herpetic keratitis may develop a recurrence.

pool.q: Argon laser trabeculoplasty is appropriate in the treatment of what condition?
pool.rationale: Laser trabeculoplasty (argon or selective) is indicated in the treatment of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), and secondary open-angle glaucomas such as exfoliation/pseudoexfoliation glaucoma and pigmentary glaucoma. It is contraindicated in developmental glaucomas, and in uveitic or neovascular glaucomas with or without angle closure.

pool.q: A patient presents with narrow angles and findings suspicious for iris and/or ciliary body cysts. What is the best imaging modality for further investigation?

options.b: computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits

pool.rationale: Ultrasound biomicroscopy is the best way to image the ciliary body and anterior choroid. It can help diagnose plateau iris syndrome, ciliary body cysts, and ciliary tumors. Anterior segment OCT does not have enough penetration to adequately image the ciliary body. B-scan ultrasonography is not ideal for imaging anterior structures. CT scans do not provide detailed imaging of anterior segment structures.

pool.q: A 65-year-old woman presents for evaluation of presumed normal-tension glaucoma in both eyes. Visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. She has a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.9 OU. There was a splinter hemorrhage off the right optic nerve. Intraocular pressure was 14 OU. Visual fields show mild inferior and superior arcuate defects in both eyes and a central scotoma in the right eye. What presenting finding warrants neuroimaging in this case?

options.a: splinter hemorrhage off the right optic nerve
options.c: central scotoma in the right eye

pool.rationale: Glaucoma tends to cause peripheral visual field defects, including nasal steps and inferior/superior arcuate defects. Visual acuity is not typically affected until end-state glaucoma; therefore, a central scotoma is concerning for a second process coinciding with the normal-tension glaucoma and requires neuroimaging. Optic disc splinter hemorrhages are common with glaucoma. A symmetric intraocular pressure and cup-to-disc ratio do not warrant neuroimaging.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication of cyclodestruction is unique to endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation?
pool.rationale: All cyclodestructive procedures can result in significant pain, hypotony, inflammation, cystoid macular edema, intraocular hemorrhage, and retinal detachment. Only endoscopic cyclophotocoagulation (an intraocular procedure) carries with it the additional risk of endophthalmitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of mitomycin C?
pool.rationale:
Mitomycin C is an antitumor antibiotic produced by Streptomyces caespitosus. It is a DNA alkylating agent that prevents DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. In glaucoma filtering surgery, it is used to inhibit fibroblast proliferation.
Other examples of antimetabolites (drugs that interfere with cell proliferation) are 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), which is a pyrimidine analogue, and methotrexate, which is a folic acid antagonist.
Infliximab, a TNF-alpha inhibitor, is a biologic used in the treatment of autoimmune diseases.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient develops secondary glaucoma after a penetrating corneal injury. Slit-lamp examination reveals mild corneal edema and effacement of the normal iris architecture. Argon laser applied to the abnormal iris produces white burns. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Epithelial ingrowth results from inadequate wound closure after intraocular surgery or penetrating trauma. Epithelial cells originating from the conjunctiva or cornea gain access to the anterior chamber (AC) and then proliferate, resulting in alteration of anterior segment structures. Argon laser application to the epithelial membrane produces white burns and is diagnostic of this condition; it may also be used to delineate the extent of proliferation.
Fibrous ingrowth occurs in circumstances similar to those in epithelial ingrowth, but it is caused by invasion of the AC by fibroblasts, and the resulting membrane is usually vascularized.
Cyclitic membrane arises from the ciliary body and is a complication of chronic uveitis. It is typically associated with hypotony.
Rubeosis iridis refers to iris neovascularization and does not have the clinical appearance described.

pool.q: After suffering a blunt ocular injury 13 years prior, a patient develops unilateral elevated IOP in the previously traumatized eye. What gonioscopic findings might be present on examination?

options.a: wider ciliary body band than the fellow eye
options.b: fine vessels crossing the scleral spur

pool.rationale: Angle recession is caused by a tear between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibers of the ciliary body. Gonioscopically, a widened ciliary body band compared to the fellow eye suggests angle recession. Other findings may include torn iris processes and a whiter-appearing scleral spur (due to tearing of the uveal meshwork from the surface). A densely pigmented trabecular meshwork is found in pigment dispersion syndrome. Patchy peripheral anterior synechiae can be seen in chronic angle closure, uveitis, and after laser trabeculoplasty. Fine vessels crossing the scleral spur are seen in neovascular glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the pattern of iris transillumination in exfoliation syndrome?
pool.rationale: Iris transillumination defects can be seen in a variety of conditions. In exfoliation syndrome, iris transillumination defects occur at the pupillary margin. Midperipheral spoke-like iris transillumination defects are seen in pigment dispersion syndrome due to rubbing of iris pigment epithelium against the zonular fibers. Diffuse and sectoral transillumination defects are seen in albinism and herpetic disease, respectively.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what type of lens-induced secondary glaucoma is the lens capsule most likely to be found intact?
pool.rationale:
Phacolytic glaucoma results from the leakage of lens proteins through microscopic openings in an intact lens capsule, in the setting of a hypermature cataract. The lens material and phagocytizing macrophages block the trabecular meshwork.
Lens particle glaucoma results from free cortical material following capsule violation from surgery, trauma, or capsulotomy. Phacoantigenic glaucoma results from free retained lens material following surgery or trauma as well. However, in phacoantigenic glaucoma, the patient is sensitized to the lens material and develops granulomatous inflammation.
With a vitrectomy, there is a chance that the posterior lens capsule can be damaged during the procedure, in turn leading to leakage of lens protein, causing phacoantigenic or lens particle glaucoma.

pool.q: A patient underwent transscleral cyclophotocoagulation in the left eye and presented a week later with decreased visual acuity in that eye from 20/200 to 20/400. He denied eye pain. His intraocular pressure was 22 mm Hg. The slit-lamp examination revealed a deep and quiet anterior chamber. The fundus examination was unremarkable except for a blunted foveal reflex. What is the likely cause of vision loss in this patient?
pool.rationale: Cystoid macular edema is thought to be the predominant cause of vision loss after transscleral cyclophotocoagulation. Cyclodestructive procedures target the ciliary processes, damaging the cells that produce aqueous humor. These procedures are inflammatory and commonly cause iritis and temporary discomfort. Vision-threatening complications include cystoid macular edema, prolonged hypotony, corneal decompensation, corneal graft failure, hemorrhage, phthisis bulbi, and sympathetic ophthalmia. Endoscopic cyclodestruction is contraindicated in blind eyes, because it carries a small risk of sympathetic ophthalmia, since it is an incisional surgery. In some patients, vision declines without a cause that is identifiable on examination. The other options (cataract, accommodative insufficiency, and central retinal artery occlusion) are not complications associated with transscleral cyclophotocoagulation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What intraocular pressure (IOP)-lowering agent increases trabecular outflow?
pool.rationale: Trabecular outflow is increased by miotics such as pilocarpine. Dorzolamide and timolol decrease aqueous production, and latanoprost increases uveoscleral outflow.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When using Goldmann tonometry, what corneal characteristic, aside from lower than average thickness, can cause a falsely low intraocular pressure (IOP) reading?
pool.rationale:
Goldmann tonometry measures intraocular pressure by corneal applanation. Corneal properties affecting the flexibility of the cornea can lead to inaccurate IOP readings.
Corneal edema and thinner corneas lead to falsely low IOP readings.
Corneal scars, thicker corneas, band keratopathy, and high corneal curvature lead to falsely high IOP readings.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In the CIGTS (Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study), what was the most common cause of decreased visual acuity for subjects in the surgical arm?
pool.rationale:
For most types of glaucoma (other than primary congenital glaucoma), a trial of medication and/or laser surgery is first attempted to control IOP. The clinician must exercise caution when recommending incisional surgery because potential adverse effects (infections, hypotony, cataracts) can result in vision loss. Early studies of trabeculectomy as initial therapy for glaucoma, which were performed before the introduction of contemporary glaucoma medications, suggested that trabeculectomy might offer some advantages—better control of IOP, reduction in the number of patient visits to the physician, and possibly better preservation of the visual field, for example. The results of the Collaborative Initial Glaucoma Treatment Study (CIGTS) confirmed that initial surgical therapy achieves better IOP control than does initial medical therapy. However, this finding did not translate to better visual field stabilization on average because subjects who received initial surgical treatment had a higher risk of cataract in the long term.
Other results from CIGTS: Patients in the surgical arm complained of more local irritation, but this was not related to vision loss. Postoperative complications such as endophthalmitis were not a significant cause of vision loss in the surgery arm. Dry eye did not account for any visual differences between the 2 groups.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What change in refractive error is typical in a patient taking pilocarpine?
pool.rationale: Myopia caused by induced ciliary muscle contraction is a common side effect of all cholinergic agents. This mechanism also causes headache/brow ache (from ciliary muscle spasm) in patients on pilocarpine therapy. Other long-term side effects of pilocarpine include retinal detachment, cataract formation, iris pigment epithelial cysts, epiphora (lacrimal stimulation and punctal stenosis), and ocular surface changes (drug-induced pseudopemphigoid).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What operative retina vitreous procedure can result in non-pupillary block angle closure?

options.b: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injection

pool.rationale:
Anterior choroidal effusions causing forward rotation of the ciliary body and angle closure can occur after scleral buckling procedures and extensive panretinal photocoagulation. Medical management with cycloplegics and aqueous suppression is often adequate until the effusions resolve.
The placement of expansile gas or silicone oil can cause angle closure through forward movement of the lens and pupillary block. In general, choroidal effusions are not present. In these cases, an inferior iridectomy may help. Less commonly, the gas or oil may have to be removed.
Anti-VEGF injections can cause elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), but the angle is open.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Comparing ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) to conventional ophthalmic ultrasonography, what are the differences in wavelength, scleral penetration, and resolution?

options.a: UBM uses longer-wavelength sound waves and has greater scleral penetration and increased resolution.
options.b: UBM uses longer-wavelength sound waves and has less scleral penetration and decreased resolution.
options.c: UBM uses shorter-wavelength sound waves and has less scleral penetration and increased resolution.
options.d: UBM uses shorter-wavelength sound waves and has greater scleral penetration and decreased resolution.

pool.rationale: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) employs shorter-wavelength sound waves as compared to conventional ocular ultrasonography, providing increased resolution but with limited penetration through the sclera. It allows for detailed examination of the anterior and posterior chambers and the ciliary body. Another modality used to evaluate the anterior segment is anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT), which provides better resolution than UBM; however, it has minimal scleral penetration, limiting the ability to provide images of the ciliary body and adjacent structures.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Unilateral glaucoma with corneal edema in a young woman with no history of trauma is suspicious for what condition?
pool.rationale:
Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome is characterized by abnormal corneal endothelium that has epithelium-like characteristics and extends from the peripheral cornea onto the trabecular meshwork and iris. It causes a secondary angle-closure glaucoma. There are 3 variants (essential [progressive] iris atrophy, Chandler syndrome, and Cogan-Reese syndrome), with varying amounts of corneal and iris changes. The Chandler variant of ICE syndrome is characterized by corneal edema. ICE syndrome is almost always unilateral and is more common in women.
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is characterized by iris changes similar to those in ICE syndrome, and 50% of persons with this syndrome develop glaucoma. However, unlike ICE syndrome, the disease is bilateral and the peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) insert into a prominent Schwalbe line with no extension beyond it.
Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy is characterized by bilateral endothelial changes including vesicles, bands, and geographic opacities. Many affected individuals are asymptomatic. Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and iris abnormalities (corectopia and PAS) can occur in this condition but are not common.
Fuchs dystrophy is an endothelial dystrophy with findings ranging from asymptomatic central corneal guttae to cornea edema and painful bullous keratopathy. It is more common in women with onset after 50 years of age and is not associated with glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Among glaucomas associated with intraocular inflammation, for what condition are corticosteroids generally ineffective?
pool.rationale: Inflammatory glaucomas comprise a wide range of disorders that can cause intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation from edema of the trabecular meshwork, trabecular meshwork endothelial cell dysfunction, blockage of the trabecular meshwork by fibrin and inflammatory cells or peripheral anterior synechiae. In the setting of inflammation, corticosteroids are often a mainstay of treatment in addition to aqueous suppressants. Glaucomatocyclitic crisis in particular responds very well to topical corticosteroids. On the other hand, Fuchs uveitis syndrome (formerly Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis) responds poorly to corticosteroids. Since IOP does not correlate to the degree of inflammation in this condition, it is not necessary to treat the inflammation, and management should focus on medical and/or surgical pressure control.

pool.q: An 85-year-old pseudophakic woman requires surgery for advanced primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) that is not controlled with maximum tolerated medical therapy. What factor in the patient's history could be a relative contraindication for trabeculectomy in this patient?

options.b: history of clear corneal cataract surgery

pool.rationale:
Surgical glaucoma treatment in the elderly requires consideration of several issues specific to this patient population. The need for surgery should first be evaluated based on the severity of the disease, the risk of functional visual loss, the life expectancy of the patient, and the general condition and ability of the patient to withstand the stress of surgery. For trabeculectomy in particular, other considerations include the ability to adhere to the postoperative medical regimen, the ability to keep follow-up appointments, and the possibility of compromised healing, because the tissue of older patients is thinner and more fragile than that of younger patients. Frequent follow-up visits are critical in the postoperative management of trabeculectomy and therefore this procedure is best avoided if a patient is unable to come to the clinic for postoperative care.
There is no specific age cut-off for the consideration of trabeculectomy.  The success rate of trabeculectomy is lower in patients with cataract surgery via a scleral tunnel incision. Controlled hypertension is not a contraindication for glaucoma surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What optic disc characteristic is most specific for glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Glaucomatous cups are associated with both generalized and focal ophthalmologic signs. General signs include large optic cup, asymmetry of the optic cups, and progressive enlargement of the cup. Focal signs include notching of the rim, vertical elongation of the cup, cupping to the rim margin, retinal nerve fiber layer hemorrhage, and nerve fiber layer loss. Less specific signs are also observed, including exposed lamina cribrosa, nasal displacement of rim vessels, baring of circumlinear vessels, and peripapillary atrophy.



(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of indirect parasympathomimetics in the treatment of glaucoma?

options.a: suppression of acetylcholine release from nerve terminals
options.b: increased sensitivity of post-synaptic nerve terminals to acetylcholine
options.c: inhibition of enzyme that inactivates acetylcholine

pool.rationale:
Indirect parasympathomimetics, such as echothiophate, are inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase. They inactivate cholinesterase and inhibit the enzymatic destruction of acetylcholine, leaving it free to act on its receptors.
Direct parasympathomimetics, such as pilocarpine and carbachol, directly stimulate muscarinic receptors in the same way as acetylcholine does.
Botulinum toxin causes suppression of acetylcholine release from nerve terminals. When used in small amounts, its muscle-weakening effect is helpful in the treatment of conditions such as blepharospasm.

pool.q: An 85-year-old woman had a laser peripheral iridotomy 2 days ago for acute angle closure, but her intraocular pressure is still elevated. She has mild cataracts in both eyes. What is your next step in management?

options.a: Check for patency of iridotomy and repeat laser if it is not patent.
options.b: Perform cataract surgery for phacomorphic glaucoma.
options.c: Administer topical steroids for phacolytic glaucoma.
options.d: Perform synechiolysis for chronic angle-closure glaucoma.

pool.rationale:
Of the nearly 67 million patients with glaucoma worldwide, it has been estimated that one-half are affected by angle closure. Occurring less often in the West, it is the predominant form of glaucoma in East Asia. The presentation of angle closure can be acute, with profound symptoms, or chronic, with asymptomatic visual loss.
The patient does not have a large lens, which could cause phacomorphic glaucoma, or a mature cataract, which could cause phacolytic glaucoma. She has acute, not chronic, angle closure. The most likely cause of persistent symptoms of angle closure following iridotomy in this patient is an iridotomy that is not patent. The procedure should be repeated if it is not patent.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with a peripherally and centrally shallow anterior chamber (AC) and increased intraocular pressure (IOP) after panretinal photocoagulation for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. In addition to aqueous suppression, what is an appropriate step in initial management?

options.d: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injection

pool.rationale:
Angle closure after panretinal photocoagulation results from ciliary body swelling with anterior rotation of the lens-iris diaphragm. The AC is shallow both centrally and peripherally. Cycloplegia causes posterior movement of the iris-lens diaphragm, resulting in deepening of the AC.
Laser iridotomy is not helpful, since there is no pupillary block. Laser iridoplasty may help to minimize iridocorneal contact but is not the first step in management. Anti-VEGF injection is not helpful in addressing the mechanism of angle closure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the advantage of trabeculotomy ab externo over goniotomy for treatment of congenital glaucoma?

options.b: can be performed with an opacified cornea

pool.rationale:
In trabeculotomy ab externo, a conjunctival flap is created first, followed by dissection of a partial thickness scleral flap. The Schlemm canal is then cannulated with either a Trabeculotome or a polypropylene suture (with or without the help of an illuminated catheter). This procedure can be performed with an opacified cornea.
Goniotomy is performed from an ab interno (anterior chamber) approach. A needle-knife is passed through a corneal incision and across the anterior chamber to the opposite angle. A superficial incision is then made in the anterior aspect of the trabecular meshwork under gonioscopic guidance, which requires a clear cornea for visualization.
Goniotomy takes less time to perform than trabeculotomy. Both procedures are typically performed in the pediatric age group under general anesthesia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What topical glaucoma medication can exacerbate chronic angle-closure glaucoma (ACG)?
pool.rationale:
Pilocarpine is a nonselective muscarinic parasympathomimetic agent that can exacerbate angle closure by causing pupillary block, especially at higher-strength concentrations and with prolonged use. This occurs by increased vascular congestion of the iris and/or by rotating the lens-iris interface more anteriorly.
Apraclonidine, a sympathomimetic agent (α-2 and weak α-1 adrenergic agonist), is a medication used for short-term intraocular pressure (IOP) control. Brimonidine is also an α-2 adrenergic agonist with longer potential for IOP control in glaucoma patients.

pool.q: What is the definitive surgical treatment for aqueous misdirection?

options.c: pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloido-zonulectomy and iridectomy

pool.rationale: Aqueous misdirection is a rare form of glaucoma that most commonly occurs after ocular surgery in patients with a history of angle closure. Medical management and laser iridotomy may control aqueous misdirection in around 50% of cases; the other half require surgical intervention. In aphakic and pseudophakic eyes, the anterior vitreous can be disrupted with Nd:YAG laser. Laser photocoagulation of the ciliary processes may also help. However, the definitive surgical treatment is pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloido-zonulectomy and iridectomy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What would be the most appropriate initial medical therapy for a 35-year-old patient with moderate glaucoma and a history of asthma?
pool.rationale:
Prostaglandin analogs and topical beta blockers are often used as initial therapy because they can achieve a 20%-30% intraocular pressure (IOP) reduction with once-daily dosing. In this patient, latanoprost, travoprost, or bimatoprost are all reasonable options.
Nonselective beta blockers (such as timolol) should be avoided in patients with reactive airway disease, as they can cause bronchospasm. Nonselective beta blockers should also be used with caution in patients with hypotension, bradycardia, and heart block. Betaxolol is a selective β1antagonist, making it safer to use in patients with asthma; however, it is less effective than nonselective beta blockers. Brimonidine can also achieve good pressure reduction, but is generally used as second- or third-line therapy, due to the need for 2-3X/day dosing and higher rate of allergy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Most cases of juvenile-onset open-angle glaucoma (JOAG) are inherited in what way?
pool.rationale: Most cases of JOAG are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Patients can present between 4 and 35 years of age, with elevated IOP and normal-appearing angles. The myocilin gene, formerly named TIGR (the trabecular meshwork inducible glucocorticoid response gene), was first linked to chromosome 1q21-31. Five loci are now mapped for JOAG.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What mechanism may result in angle closure after either scleral buckling or panretinal photocoagulation?
pool.rationale: Uveal effusion or uveal hemorrhage refers to fluid or blood in the potential space between the uvea (choroid and ciliary body) and the sclera. Causes include certain sulfonamide medications, panretinal photocoagulation, inflammation, infection, penetrating surgery, scleral buckle surgery, trauma, retinal vein occlusion, tumor, and uveal effusion syndrome. The suprachoroidal or supraciliary mass effect may result in secondary angle closure related to forward displacement of the lens–iris interface. Expansile gases and silicone oil used in vitreoretinal surgery may lead to non-pupillary block angle closure. Neovascularization also causes secondary angle closure without pupillary block, but it is not precipitated by panretinal photocoagulation or scleral buckling. Similarly, aqueous misdirection is not caused by panretinal photocoagulation or scleral buckle procedure.

pool.q: A 62-year-old man with a history of trabeculectomy in the right eye 1 year prior presents with pain and decreased vision in the right eye. On examination, he has diffuse conjunctival hyperemia, purulent material within the bleb, and 2+ cell in the anterior chamber and vitreous cavity. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.a: intravitreal antibiotics with or without pars plana vitrectomy

pool.rationale: This patient has bleb-related endophthalmitis, which often occurs many years after trabeculectomy. While blebitis is characterized by mucopurulent infiltrate within the bleb, localized conjunctival hyperemia, and minimal to no intraocular inflammation, bleb-related endophthalmitis has more diffuse conjunctival hyperemia, purulent material within the bleb, and prominent anterior chamber inflammation. A hypopyon or vitritis may also be present. While blebitis may be treated with topical or subconjunctival antibiotics, bleb-related endophthalmitis is treated like other types of endophthalmitis, with intravitreal injection of antibiotics. Because organisms associated with bleb-related endophthalmitis are often more virulent, early vitrectomy may be considered. Topical steroids alone are not appropriate for treating endophthalmitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a nonglaucomatous disc, what quadrant of the neural rim is generally the thickest?
pool.rationale: The physiologic neural rim is typically the broadest inferiorly, followed by the superior, nasal, and temporal rims. This is commonly referred to as the ISNT (inferior, superior, nasal, temporal) rule. Inferior rim thinning in the absence of field loss should be considered suspicious and might represent early glaucoma. Any violation of the ISNT rule should be considered as a potential indicator of early glaucoma or glaucoma suspect.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An infant is scheduled for an examination under anesthesia. What anesthetic agent would have the least effect on the infant's intraocular pressure (IOP)?
pool.rationale: Most anesthetics have an effect on IOP measurements. Sevoflurane and many others lower IOP, whereas ketamine and succinylcholine (not really an anesthetic agent, but a skeletal muscle relaxant adjunct to general anesthesia) may increase IOP. Chloral hydrate has been shown to have no effect on IOP measurement.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What retinal procedure carries the highest risk of secondary angle closure due to choroidal effusion and anterior rotation of the ciliary body?
pool.rationale:
Choroidal effusion and ciliary body swelling have the greatest likelihood of developing after scleral buckling procedures and to a lesser degree after panretinal photocoagulation. Used for surgical repair of retinal detachments, scleral buckles, especially the encircling bands, can produce shallowing of the anterior chamber angle and frank angle closure, often accompanied by choroidal effusion and anterior rotation of the ciliary body, causing a flattening of the peripheral iris with a relatively deep central anterior chamber. Usually, the anterior chamber deepens with opening of the anterior chamber angle over days to weeks with medical therapy consisting of cycloplegics, anti-inflammatory agents, β-adrenergic antagonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and hyperosmotic agents. If medical management is unsuccessful, argon laser iridoplasty, drainage of suprachoroidal fluid, or adjustment of the scleral buckle may be required. Iridectomy is usually of little benefit in this condition. The scleral buckle can impede venous drainage by compressing a vortex vein, elevating episcleral venous pressure and IOP. Such cases may respond only to moving the scleral buckle or releasing tension on the encircling band.
Topical therapy with cycloplegics, anti-inflammatory agents, and hypotensive drops may be therapeutic in treating a secondary angle closure episode. Expansile gases can cause angle closure from gas overfill, causing anterior compression of the lens-iris diaphragm or pupillary block. Silicone oil can cause pupillary block or can emulsify and directly obstruct the trabecular meshwork. Laser retinopexy does not typically cause secondary glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What characteristic would be most typical in a patient newly diagnosed with primary angle-closure glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is associated with a number of known risk factors. It is most common among those with Inuit or East Asian lineage, in eyes with small anterior segments and/or short axial lengths, in patients over 40, in women more than men, in patients with a known family history, and in hyperopes.

pool.q: A 7-year-old child is referred for evaluation with history of a port-wine stain involving the right eyelids and side of face. A complete ocular examination is performed, and elevated intraocular pressure is noted in the right eye. What additional testing is the most important next step in the management of this patient?
pool.rationale: There is concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, also known as encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, in this patient. There is no race or gender predilection and no inheritance pattern has been established for this condition. Genetic testing is unlikely to be helpful. Patients can also have an ipsilateral choroidal hemangioma, causing a "tomato ketchup" fundus appearance, and characterization with ICG may be useful. Most importantly, there is an association with ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma, which can lead to intracerebral calcifications, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, and a variable amount of cognitive impairment. A systemic workup with neurorimaging is therefore of key importance.

pool.q: What glaucoma drops increase the risk of corneal decompensation in a patient with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy?
pool.rationale: Dorzolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor (CAI), inhibits active secretion by blocking carbonic anhydrase in the nonpigmented ciliary epithelial cells in the epithelial processes. Corneal endothelium contains CA II isoenzyme, which is blocked by topically applied CAI. This may lead to corneal decompensation, especially in corneas with decreased endothelial cell number and function (eg, Fuchs dystrophy).

pool.q: A 67-year-old man has been followed as a glaucoma suspect. What would be the most compelling reason to begin treatment with a glaucoma medication?

options.b: progressive cupping of the optic nerves
options.d: recent diagnosis of glaucoma in a sibling

pool.rationale: Progressive cupping of the optic nerves is diagnostic of glaucoma, and IOP-lowering treatment should be initiated. A family history of glaucoma, and higher-than-average IOP, increase the risk of developing glaucoma; these factors may warrant closer monitoring of a glaucoma suspect but should not automatically lead to initiating IOP-lowering treatment. Reduced visual acuity is most likely from age-related cataract in this 67-year-old patient and is not a reason to start glaucoma therapy.

pool.q: What topical ocular hypotensive medication should be discontinued in a patient who also takes an oral monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI)?
pool.rationale:
Brimonidine is a relatively selective α2-adrenergic agonist. It lowers intraocular pressure (IOP) by decreasing aqueous production and increasing uveoscleral outflow.
Combined with MAOIs, topical brimonidine can lead to excessive norepinephrine and hypertensive crisis caused by the interference of the MAOIs with the metabolism of brimonidine. This can occur with apraclonidine as well.
Systemic side effects of brimonidine include oral dryness, sedation, drowsiness, headache, and fatigue, and the medication should be avoided in children younger than 5 years of age because of the risk of central nervous system depression.
Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog and does not have known interactions with MAOI medications; timolol, a beta-blocker, and dorzolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, also are not known to interact with MAOIs.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 25-year-old woman has unilateral glaucomatous disc cupping. Her past ocular history includes blunt trauma to that eye in her teens, which resulted in transient vision loss that was fully recovered after about a week. Gonioscopy is most likely to reveal what finding?

options.b: iridocorneal adhesions to a posterior embryotoxon
options.c: patchy, increased pigmentation of trabecular meshwork
options.d: deepened angle recess with torn iris processes

pool.rationale:
Angle-recession or traumatic glaucoma is a chronic, typically unilateral, secondary open-angle glaucoma (OAG) that may occur soon after trauma or develop months to years later. Angle recession results from a tear between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibers of the ciliary body. The typical gonioscopic appearance is that of a broad angle recess with absent or torn iris processes and a white, prominent scleral spur. Angle recession should be suspected in a patient presenting with unilateral IOP elevation, whether or not the patient recalls a history of trauma.
Pigmentary glaucoma is most commonly seen in young, myopic males and is characterized by dense, homogeneous pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork.
Patchy, heavy pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork is seen in exfoliation syndrome. Exfoliation glaucoma can present unilaterally; it is rarely seen in patients younger than 50 years.
Iridocorneal adhesions to a posterior embryotoxon are seen in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, which is a bilateral condition.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause of secondary glaucoma from tumors involving the ciliary body?

options.b: anterior rotation of the ciliary body
options.d: direct invasion of the anterior chamber angle

pool.rationale: The most common cause of glaucoma in primary or metastatic tumors of the ciliary body is direct invasion of the anterior chamber angle. All the other mechanisms listed (tumor-laden macrophage, neovascularization, and anterior rotation of the ciliary body) can also result in secondary glaucoma, but less commonly.

pool.q: What is the treatment for a patient with elevated intraocular pressure and continued risk of angle closure despite patent peripheral iridotomy in plateau iris syndrome?
pool.rationale:
Plateau iris syndrome management initially includes either laser iridotomy to eliminate any component of pupillary block, or lensectomy can be considered if a cataract is present. Despite both of these treatments, plateau iris patients are at continued risk of angle closure secondary to the anterior insertion of the zonules on ciliary processes. Laser peripheral iridoplasty or argon gonioplasty is indicated in patients with a continued presence of a narrow angle despite patent iridotomy.
Argon or selective laser trabeculoplasty would not decrease risk of angle closure. Repeat laser iridotomy would be indicated if the initial iridotomy had failed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 80-year-old woman presents with a red, painful eye with markedly elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), and prominent cell and flare. There are no keratic precipitates. The anterior chamber is deep. She has mature cataracts bilaterally and wrinkling of the lens capsule. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
This patient likely has a secondary open-angle glaucoma, given the deep chamber. Gonioscopy should be attempted but may be difficult through a cornea with diffuse microcystic edema from the significantly elevated IOP. Given the age of the patient and the characteristics of the cataracts, she likely has a lens-induced glaucoma. There are 3 entities: phacolytic glaucoma, lens particle glaucoma, and phacoantigenic glaucoma. Phacolytic is an inflammatory glaucoma resulting from leakage of high-molecular-weight lens protein through microscopic openings in the capsule of a mature or hypermature cataract that subsequently obstructs the trabecular meshwork. The wrinkling of the capsule is one clue that favors phacolytic glaucoma. Additionally, the lack of keratic precipitates differentiates phacolytic glaucoma from phacoantigenic glaucoma. Cellular debris may be seen layered in the anterior chamber angle, and a pseudohypopyon may be present.
This is not lens particle glaucoma, because this patient has not had cataract extraction or trauma that would have released a lens particle into the anterior chamber. Phacoantigenic glaucoma also occurs after surgery or penetrating trauma and is associated with a granulomatous inflammation. Patients become sensitized to their own lens protein. Although there are varied presentations, most patients will have a moderate anterior chamber reaction with keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium and the anterior lens surface. A low-grade vitritis, posterior synechiae and peripheral anterior synechiae, and residual lens material may be present. Herpes zoster can be considered; however, given the whole clinical picture, phacolytic glaucoma is most likely.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of glaucoma medications can induce uterine smooth muscle contraction and should therefore be avoided during pregnancy?
pool.rationale:
Prostaglandin analogues (PGAs) are prodrugs that are hydrolyzed in the cornea to prostaglandin F2a (PGF2a), which reduces intraocular pressure. Systemically, PGF2a affects uterine smooth muscle and induces contraction. Although the systemic absorption of PGAs is minimal, they are best avoided in pregnancy due to their potential to induce labor.
However, in several studies, it was seen that Propranolol could induce contractions in the pregnant uterine musculature. Please see https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3879864/ Published online 2013 Nov 10 PMID: 24392402 Comparison Effect of Oral Propranolol and Oxytocin Versus Oxytocin Only on Induction of Labour in Nulliparous Women (A Double Blind Randomized Trial).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What percent of glaucoma patients develop a retinal nerve fiber layer hemorrhage at some point during the course of the disease?
pool.rationale: At some point during the course of the disease, 30% of glaucoma patients develop a retinal nerve fiber layer hemorrhage. The hemorrhages usually clear over 3 weeks to 3 months.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) is absolutely contraindicated in what scenario?
pool.rationale: Laser trabeculoplasty (SLT or ALT) requires an open angle for proper treatment. A closed angle (appositional or synechial) is an absolute contraindication, and similarly the presence of extensive PAS is also a strong contraindication to this procedure, though it could be considered in an angle with only intermittent PAS, avoiding those areas. In the setting of an open angle, history of anterior uveitis is an additional relative contraindication; however, it can be used if the uveitis is well controlled, and steroid response is thought to be the main issue. Previous ALT is not a contraindication to treatment with SLT.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 64-year-old patient, who has a history of chronic angle-closure glaucoma, undergoes a trabeculectomy and the next day has eye pain, nausea, and vomiting. A clinical examination shows an intraocular pressure of 48 mm Hg, a low bleb, a shallow anterior chamber, and an attached retina. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.d: laser suture lysis and bleb needling

pool.rationale:
Malignant glaucoma, also known as aqueous misdirection, can be diagnosed when the intraocular pressure is high, the anterior chamber is flat, and an open peripheral iridectomy is present (which should eliminate pupillary block). Malignant glaucoma can be medically managed in 50% of patients who have an open iridotomy or iridectomy. Immediate treatment of these patients includes: aqueous suppression (β-adrenergic antagonists, α2-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors); intensive cycloplegic therapy (atropine); and systemic hyperosmotic agents to shrink the vitreous.  Definitive treatment is pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloido-zonulectomy combined with an anterior chamber-deepening procedure. However, given the risk of surgery, nonsurgical management should be attempted first.
Argon laser iridoplasty is useful in managing eyes with appositional angles despite a patent PI in patients with plateau iris and phacomorphic angle narrowing, but it does not correct the underlying issue in patients with malignant glaucoma.
Laser suture lysis and bleb needling would be performed for a early and late fibrosis of the sclerostomy site and conjunctiva, respectively.
Posterior scleral windows are useful in non-resolving choroidal effusions, but do not improve malignant glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For a patient who develops aqueous misdirection (ie, malignant glaucoma) after cataract surgery, initial management would include what therapy?

options.a: laser disruption of the anterior hyaloid face

pool.rationale: Initial medical therapy typically includes aqueous suppressants and cycloplegia, which may break or moderate an episode of malignant glaucoma or aqueous misdirection. If this therapy fails to elicit acceptable control of the intraocular pressure (IOP), then yttrium-aluminum-garnet (YAG) iridotomy may be performed, along with disruption of the anterior vitreous face in aphakic or pseudophakic patients. While medical management and laser iridotomy control malignant glaucoma in approximately half of patients, the rest will require surgical treatment. In these patients, pars plana vitrectomy with anterior hyaloido-zonulo-iridectomy is the definitive surgical treatment. Miotics are contraindicated and may worsen the episode.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Over the past year, a 50-year-old woman has complained of frequent headaches that radiate from around her left eye. She has worn over-the-counter reading glasses for the last decade, but has not had an eye examination since childhood. She states that she has no eye problems, but her internist has recommended a baseline eye evaluation. What diagnostic test is most important to evaluate for this patient?
pool.rationale:
Subacute intermittent angle-closure glaucoma is frequently asymptomatic but may present with various symptoms, including frequent headaches and intermittent episodes of blurry vision, halos, and eye pain. In this case, gonioscopy is the most helpful test because it is the only one among those listed that can identify angle closure and lead to the treatment of choice, namely, laser peripheral iridotomy.
Although tonometry and pachymetry can provide useful information for this patient, they are not diagnostic for angle closure.
Topography is not relevant in this clinical scenario.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the critical slit-lamp finding in phacolytic glaucoma?

options.a: keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium
options.c: large cells with debris and flare in the anterior chamber

pool.rationale: Phacolytic glaucoma is a complication of a mature or hypermature cataract in which denatured, high-molecular weight lens proteins leak through an intact but permeable lens capsule and induce inflammation and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). The clinical presentation is typically an abrupt onset of pain and redness in an eye with prolonged poor vision. White debris and flare are typical, but keratic precipitates, if found, are nonspecific. Phacolytic glaucoma is a form of secondary open-angle glaucoma. On gonioscopy, the angle is unaffected and usually of normal depth.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 22-year-old myopic male presents with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 35 mm Hg OD and 20 mm Hg OS. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment is normal and gonioscopy shows open angles in both eyes. The C:D ratio is 0.8, with a thin inferior rim OD, and is 0.7 OS, with a uniform rim. Visual field testing shows a superior field defect OD and is normal OS. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) shows thin retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) OU.  What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
JOAG is a form of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) that presents between the ages of 4 and 35 years. It is characterized by elevated IOP and normal angle appearance. JOAG is usually inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Due to the later age of onset, it does not cause corneal enlargement or Haab striae.
Ocular hypertension refers to elevated IOP without glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) presents in earlier childhood than JOAG and may present within the first month (newborn PCG), within the first 2 years of life (infantile PCG), or after 2 years of age (late-diagnosed PCG). Until 3 to 4 years of age, elevated IOP causes the cornea and globe to stretch, and this leads to the findings seen in PCG, such as corneal enlargement, Haab striae, and buphthalmos.
Pigmentary glaucoma is usually seen in young to middle-aged (20 to 50 years of age) male myopes. It is associated with anterior segment findings such as pigment on the corneal endothelium, iris transillumination defects, and hyperpigmentation of the trabecular meshwork.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What gonioscopic finding is associated with pseudoexfoliation?

options.b: inability to visualize trabecular meshwork without compression
options.c: reflux of blood into the Schlemm canal

pool.rationale: Narrow angles and angle closure are more common in pseudoexfoliation syndrome. This is presumably due to anterior lens movement secondary to zonular weakness or dialysis. A prominent ciliary body band is often seen in patients with high myopia or prior eye trauma. Reflux of blood into the Schlemm canal is seen in patients with increased episcleral venous pressure. Iris processes crossing scleral spur are often seen in normal eyes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with normal-tension glaucoma and treatment is initiated. What should the target intraocular pressure (IOP) percent reduction be for this patient?
pool.rationale: Normal-tension (low-tension) glaucoma is thought to be multifactorial in its etiology, and the mechanism for disease progression is not fully understood. However, results from the Collaborative Normal-Tension Glaucoma Study (CNTGS) demonstrate that aggressive IOP lowering can lessen the risk of progression in these patients over a 5-year period. The study aimed for at least 30% IOP reduction from baseline, and in those patients, the risk of visual field progression was decreased from 35% to 12%. A caveat of this finding is that about half of patients who did not receive treatment over the 5-year period did not progress, making it likely that IOP is not the only factor in the development and progression of normal-tension glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of glaucoma medications can induce corneal edema in patients with poor endothelial function?
pool.rationale: Carbonic anhydrase is found in the corneal endothelium as well as the ciliary epithelium. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can induce corneal edema in patients with already compromised endothelial function.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What commonly used glaucoma procedure affects intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous production?
pool.rationale: Most glaucoma medications function by decreasing aqueous production while most glaucoma surgeries function by increasing aqueous outflow. Cyclophotocoagulation is an exception to this modality-mechanism relationship. Laser energy is applied through the sclera to the ciliary processes to decrease aqueous production. Overtreatment can lead to hypotony, which is a serious complication that can lead to vision loss. Laser trabeculoplasty results in increased aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork. Trabeculectomy and tube shunts increase aqueous outflow through alternate pathways.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the general principle by which optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) is able to image blood vessels in the retina?

options.a: Moving erythrocytes create flow voids that are detectable by low-coherence interferometry.
options.b: The improved spatial resolution and image acquisition speed of spectral domain OCT allows for direct imaging of the blood vessel walls.
options.c: Differences in the backscattered OCT signal at the same cross-section of repeated OCT B scans are thought to represent the movement of erythrocytes.
options.d: Erythrocytes reflect a characteristic wavelength of light that is different from other retinal tissues, allowing localization of blood vessels.

pool.rationale:
Differences in the backscattered OCT signal at the same cross-section of repeated OCT B scans are thought to represent the movement of erythrocytes and allow imaging of blood vessels.
Although spectral domain OCT does allow for finer resolution, it does not have the resolution to outline the small vasculature of the retina. OCT works by low-coherence interferometry (it measures backscattered light, analogous to B-scan ultrasound imaging) and does not differentiate based on recognizing any particular cell or structure. Flow voids are seen in magnetic resonance imaging of blood vessels, not in OCT angiography.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the average rate of aqueous formation?
pool.rationale: The rate of aqueous formation is 2–2.5 microliters per minute with a total aqueous volume of 250 microliters, turning over about every 1.5 to 2 hours.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the relative risk of primary open angle glaucoma (POAG) in siblings of patients with POAG?
pool.rationale: In the Baltimore Eye Survey, the relative risk of POAG increased approximately 3.7- fold for individuals who had a sibling with POAG. Increased risk of glaucoma within families is likely based on genetics, although simple mendelian inheritance of glaucoma is not common. Many cases appear to be influenced by environmental factors, with the onset being later or variable. It is therefore  important to obtain a thorough family history of glaucoma in newly diagnosed patients or glaucoma suspects, because family history is a main risk factor in the development of glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Based on the results of multiple studies, including randomized trials, what can be said about the benefit of performing a laser iridotomy for patients with pigment dispersion syndrome?

options.a: Studies have failed to show a benefit.
options.b: Studies have demonstrated a mild but statistically significant disadvantage.
options.c: Studies have demonstrated a clinically and statistically significant benefit.
options.d: Studies have demonstrated a mild but statistically significant benefit.

pool.rationale:
Laser peripheral iridotomy has been proposed as a means of minimizing posterior bowing of the iris by alleviating the pressure differential between the anterior chamber and the posterior chamber. However, multiple studies, including randomized trials, have failed to show a benefit of laser iridotomy for treatment of this condition.
Medical treatment is often successful in reducing elevated IOP in pigment dispersion syndrome.
Most patients respond reasonably well to laser trabeculoplasty, although its effect may be short-lived.
Filtering surgery is usually successful; however, extra care is warranted in young myopic male patients, who are at increased risk for hypotony maculopathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What iris color is least likely to darken with chronic prostaglandin use?
pool.rationale: Darkening of the iris is a permanent change that can occur as a result of prostaglandin use (risk of up to 33% after 5 years of use). Up to 85% of patients with green-brown and hazel (yellow-brown) irides may be affected, as opposed to only 8% with blue irides. Brown irides darken at a higher rate than blue irides, but the change is often not noticeable to the patient.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old African American man with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 26 mm Hg by applanation tonometry is referred to an ophthalmologist. The cup-to-disc ratio is 0.6 OU, with a uniform rim. The visual field and average retinal nerve fiber layer thickness are normal. What additional test is most important to perform in order to determine this patient's risk of developing glaucoma?
pool.rationale:
Central corneal thickness (CCT) has been shown to be a predictive risk factor for the development of glaucoma in patients with ocular hypertension. Corneal pachymetry is the most important test to perform at this point because it provides further information about this patient's risk profile and will impact clinical decisions such as follow-up frequency and consideration of IOP-lowering therapy.
Stereo disc photos provide objective, baseline documentation of the optic nerve and are helpful in monitoring patients. However, obtaining disc photos does not assist in the initial management of this patient's condition, and therefore is less important than measuring CCT.
Corneal topography and anterior segment OCT do not provide information relevant to this clinical situation and are not indicated.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Laser trabeculoplasty is most likely to be effective in a patient with what diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Laser trabeculoplasty is less likely to be effective in patients with iridocorneal endothelial syndrome, neovascular glaucoma, or developmental glaucoma than in patients with pseudoexfoliative glaucoma. Changes to the angle inhibit the efficacy of the laser treatment. Patients with open angles (POAG, pigmentary glaucoma, pseudoexfoliative glaucoma) are good candidates for trabeculoplasty. The energy of the laser must be titrated to the pigmentation of the angle (more pigment equals less energy) to prevent postoperative pressure spikes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the overall population based prevalence of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) in black persons, as compared with white persons?

options.a: 1–1.5 times higher among black individuals than white individuals.
options.b: 4–5 times higher among black individuals than white individuals.
options.c: 4-5 times higher among white individuals than black individuals.
options.d: 1–1.5 times higher among white individuals than black individuals.

pool.rationale: In the Baltimore Eye Survey, the prevalence of POAG among white individuals ranged from 0.9% in those aged 40–49 years to 2.2% in those aged ≥80 years, whereas the prevalence among black individuals ranged from 1.2% to 11.3%, respectively. The overall population- based prevalence was 4–5 times higher among black individuals than white individuals.In the Rotterdam Study, a longitudinal population-based study of northern Europeans, the observed prevalence was 1.1% among subjects ≥55 years of age. In the same study co-hort, the incident risk of developing glaucoma at 10 years was 2.8%. In both the Baltimore Eye Survey and the Rotterdam Study, half of the subjects with glaucoma were unaware of their diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Frequency-doubling stimuli preferentially activate what class of retinal cells?
pool.rationale:
The high temporal frequency and low spatial frequency of frequency-doubling stimuli preferentially activate the magnocellular pathway. Magnocellular neurons (M cells) are thought to be damaged early in glaucoma, and so frequency-doubling technology (FDT) perimetry may identify early defects better than white-on-white perimetry.
Parvocellular neurons (P cells) and koniocellular neurons (bistratified cells) are also retinal ganglion cells in the visual pathway. Bipolar cells send signals from the photoreceptors to the ganglion cells. None of these cells are targeted by any visual field strategy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What treatment for dry eye can raise intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale: Steroids, including Lotemax, should be used with caution in any patient with glaucoma. Patients with primary open-angle glaucoma or a family history of glaucoma are more susceptible to corticosteroid-induced IOP elevation than the general population. Any chronic corticosteroid therapy, including weak preparations such as Lotemax, fluorometholone (FML) and loteprednol (Alrex), can elevate IOP in a patient with glaucoma. If corticosteroid treatment is necessary, it is important to regularly monitor the IOP to prevent glaucomatous damage from unrecognized pressure elevations. Punctal plugs, cyclosporine, and flaxseed oil can be used safely in glaucoma patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what ethnic group is acute angle-closure glaucoma most prevalent?
pool.rationale: Alaskan Inuits have the highest known prevalence of primary angle-closure glaucoma. East Asians also have a high prevalence of this disease and make up the majority of cases worldwide.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common mechanism for intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation in eyes with retinoblastoma?

options.a: angle closure from ciliary body anterior rotation

pool.rationale: Intraocular tumors can increase intraocular pressure in several ways. The most common source of IOP elevation from primary or metastatic tumors is direct invasion of the angle. Hemolytic glaucoma may occur for tumors or treatment associated with intraocular hemorrhage, but it is less frequent than tumor infiltration. Similarly, elevated episcleral outflow may occur with extraocular extension, but it would also be relatively uncommon. Lastly, secondary angle-closure glaucoma with ciliary body rotation is less likely in this population.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An ophthalmologist who is managing a patient on-call with acutely elevated intraocular pressure of 58 mm Hg is contemplating administering oral acetazolamide to him in the clinic. On review of the patient's allergies, the ophthalmologist notices a documented "sulfa" allergy. The patient reports that he had a "rash" after taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as a child. What is the approximate chance of allergic cross-reactivity to acetazolamide in this scenario?
pool.rationale: The cross-reactivity between nonantibiotic (eg, acetazolamide) and antibiotic sulfonamide derivatives is estimated to be approximately 10%.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of visual field testing varies the stimulus intensity while keeping stimulus size constant?
pool.rationale: Automated static perimetry keeps the stimulus size constant and varies the stimulus intensity in testing. Static testing presents a stationary stimulus at various locations, varying the brightness. Frequency doubling technology perimetry (FDT) measures the ability for patients to distinguish changes in contrast. In kinetic and tangent screen testing, a target is moved into an area just until it is seen (automated or manual).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Under what condition does intraocular pressure (IOP) decrease?
pool.rationale: Several factors can increase IOP, but of the offered choices, only pregnancy is associated with lower IOP. Factors associated with increased IOP include actions that increase episcleral venous pressure, such as Valsalva maneuver, breath holding, playing a wind instrument, wearing a tight collar, bending over, and being in a supine position. Pressure on the eye, blepharospasm, and lid squeezing can also elevate IOP. In addition to pregnancy, aerobic exercise decreases IOP. Alcohol and marijuana use can also transiently decrease IOP.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of systemic medications should be avoided in a patient with anatomically narrow anterior chamber angles?
pool.rationale:
Anticholinergics can cause mild pupillary dilation that may precipitate pupillary block and angle-closure glaucoma in patients with anatomically narrow angles. These drugs should be avoided in patients who have not had peripheral iridotomies. Many drugs have anticholinergic properties, including antidepressants, antihistamines, and drugs used for incontinence.
Beta blockers should be used with caution in patients with asthma. Sulfonamides can cause uveal effusions and precipitate secondary angle closure. Corticosteroids can precipitate changes in the trabecular meshwork, causing elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). They should be avoided in patients with a diagnosis of glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular finding in iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome distinguishes it from Axenfeld-Rieger (A-R) syndrome?
pool.rationale: Both ICE syndrome and A-R syndrome are associated with corectopia, iris changes, and high peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Posterior embryotoxon is seen in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. However, endothelial abnormalities (beaten bronze appearance) and a unilateral presentation with acquired and progressive iris changes clearly distinguish ICE syndrome from A-R syndrome.

pool.q: A 67-year-old phakic hyperopic woman develops high intraocular pressure (IOP) and appositional angle closure without peripheral anterior synechiae. After laser iridotomy, the IOP remains in the high 20s on maximal tolerated medical therapy. What is the next step in management?
pool.rationale: The patient in this scenario has 3 risk factors predisposing her to angle closure (age greater than 40, hyperopia, female). Laser iridotomy did not relieve pupillary block in this patient, so the next step in treatment would be cataract removal.

pool.q: An 84-year-old Asian woman presents to the emergency room, reporting severe pain in her right eye for 4 hours. On examination, visual acuity is count fingers in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. The right eye has conjunctival injection, a steamy cornea, and mid-dilated fixed pupil. Intraocular pressure is 62 mm Hg OD and 22 mm Hg OS. The ophthalmologist determines that she has acute angle-closure glaucoma and plans to treat her high intraocular pressure with topical and systemic medication. Mannitol would have to be used with extreme caution if the patient had what medical problem?
pool.rationale:
Mannitol is a sugar alcohol used as an osmotic diuretic and weak renal vasodilator. In ophthalmology, mannitol is used to increase serum osmolality that osmotically drives fluid out of the eye to lower intraocular pressure. Osmotic agents (mannitol, glycerin, urea) should be used with caution in patients at risk for vascular volume overload, because the osmotic agent may put the patient into acute heart failure. This would include patients with congestive heart failure, angina, systemic hypertension, or recent myocardial infarction. In addition, intravenous osmotic agents can cause rapid fluid shifts within the brain and cause intracranial bleeding. Osmotic agents are cleared by the kidneys and therefore should be used with extreme caution in renally impaired patients.
Mannitol does not stimulate an increase in blood glucose and therefore is used as a low glycemic sweetener in food. Morbid obesity is not in itself a relative contraindication for mannitol. Mannitol is sometimes used as a "cutting agent" for heroin, cocaine, or methamphetamines. These illicit drugs are not in themselves a relative contraindication for mannitol.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common systemic side effect of prostaglandin analogs?
pool.rationale:
Upper respiratory tract infection/cold/flu was reported at a rate of approximately 4% and was listed as the most common systemic adverse event with clinical trials of the earliest prostaglandin analogs.
Chest pain, muscle/joint/back pain, and allergic skin reaction each occurred at a rate of 1% to 2%.
Elevated blood pressure, cognitive impairment and dry mouth are not commonly associated with prostaglandin analog therapy.

pool.q: What retinal procedure is most likely to cause angle closure due to anterior rotation of the ciliary body?
pool.rationale:
Scleral buckling procedures can cause shallow anterior chamber and angle-closure glaucoma, due to choroidal effusions and anterior rotation of the ciliary body. This can often be managed medically with cycloplegia and anti-hypertensive drugs. Panretinal photocoagulation can result in a similar situation.
Intraocular gas and silicone oil can lead to pupillary block angle closure. Silicone oil can also cause an open-angle glaucoma, owing to emulsified oil in the anterior chamber.
Pars plana vitrectomy is associated with open-angle glaucoma.
