pool.q: What glaucoma drug is classified by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as Category B in pregnancy (animal reproduction studies have failed to demonstrate a risk to the fetus and there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; or, animal studies have shown an adverse effect, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women have failed to demonstrate a risk to the fetus in any trimester)?
pool.rationale:
Brimonidine is the only commonly prescribed glaucoma medication classified as Pregnancy Category B (animal reproduction studies have failed to demonstrate a risk to the fetus and there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; or, animal studies have shown an adverse effect, but adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women have failed to demonstrate a risk to the fetus in any trimester).
Prostaglandin analogs, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs), and beta blockers are all classified Pregnancy Category C (animal reproduction studies have shown an adverse effect on the fetus and there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in humans, but potential benefits may warrant use of the drug in pregnant women despite potential risks). Although CAIs and beta blockers are category C, the oral form of these medications is used for the treatment of pseudotumor cerebri and preeclampsia, respectively, without adverse effect.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In the TVT (Tube Versus Trabeculectomy) 5-year follow-up study, eyes with previous intraocular surgery had the highest success rate with what glaucoma surgery?
pool.rationale: The 5-year follow-up study for TVT showed that, in eyes that had undergone previous intraocular surgery, the highest success rate was with Baerveldt implantation (vs trabeculectomy with MMC). Both procedures lowered IOP similarly, but patients who had the Baerveldt implant surgery required fewer additional surgical procedures.

pool.q: Long-term use of what class of medication can cause periocular hyperpigmentation, enophthalmos, deepening of the upper eyelid sulcus, and upper eyelid ptosis?
pool.rationale: Long-term use of prostaglandin analogues can cause a variety of findings, including periocular hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, enophthalmos, deepening of the upper eyelid sulcus and upper eyelid ptosis, orbital fat atrophy, inferior scleral show, and tightening of the eyelids. Steroids can have many adverse side effects, including raised intraocular pressure, but they do not cause the effects listed above. Brimonidine has a high incidence of ocular allergic reactions (follicular conjunctivitis and contact blepharodermatitis).

pool.q: Axenfeld-Rieger (A-R) syndrome has what pattern of inheritance?
pool.rationale: A-R syndrome has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. It is characterized by bilateral anomalous development of neural crest-derived anterior segment structures. A-R syndrome includes a spectrum of disorders that were formerly separated into Axenfeld anomaly, Rieger anomaly, and Rieger syndrome. Mutations in the PITX2 and FOXC1 genes have been implicated in this syndrome.

pool.q: What is the most common side effect of oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs)?
pool.rationale: Systemic side effects are very common with oral CAIs. Almost all patients develop paresthesias of the fingers and toes, usually without much functional impairment. Many patients develop fatigue and loss of appetite when using oral CAIs for more than a few days. Other common side effects include gastric burning and irritation. CAIs decrease urinary concentration of citrate and magnesium and produce temporary urinary alkalinization, which favors formation of renal calculi. This side effect usually occurs with prolonged treatment, and most calculi occur within the first 12 months of treatment. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a very rare but potentially fatal complication with oral CAIs, and patients should be warned to report skin rashes or mucous membrane changes, such as blisters or ulcers in the mouth.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What class of topical hypotensive agent should be used with caution for patients with low endothelial cell counts?
pool.rationale: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease aqueous production by antagonist activity on ciliary epithelial carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic anhydrase is also found in the corneal endothelium and is involved in endothelial pump function. Although topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors do not generally cause corneal edema, they can lead to irreversible swelling in patients with compromised endothelial cells and should be used with caution in this population. Other classes of ocular anti-hypertensives, such as prostaglandin analogs, beta-adrenergic antagonists, and alpha-adrenergic agonists do not affect corneal endothelial function.

pool.q: A patient with a history of piggyback intraocular lenses (IOL) in the left eye, both placed within the capsular bag, is referred by a local optometrist for evaluation of elevated intraocular pressure in that eye. Endothelial pigment deposition is noted on slit-lamp examination. What gonioscopic finding might be expected in this scenario?
pool.rationale:
Interlenticular opacification and iris chafing are possible complications seen with implantation of piggyback intraocular lenses within the capsular bag. Iris chafing can result in a pigment dispersion syndrome, and associated elevated intraocular pressure, presumably from obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by pigment granules. Findings associated with pigment dispersion syndrome include pigment deposits on the corneal endothelium (Krukenberg spindle), midperipheral iris transillumination defects, pigment staining of the lens capsule at the insertion of the zonular fibers (Zentmayer ring or Scheie stripe), heavy pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork, and pigment speckling at or anterior to the Schwalbe line (Sampaolesi line).
Widened ciliary body band, peripheral anterior synechiae, and posterior embryotoxon are not associated with piggyback intraocular lens placement.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What intraocular pressure (IOP)-lowering drop is preferred when glaucoma therapy must be continued during pregnancy?
pool.rationale:
Glaucoma medications have not been studied in pregnant women; therefore, none may be considered as Category A for use in pregnancy. (Category A: Adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown an increased risk of fetal abnormalities.)
Two IOP-lowering agents are in Category B: Brimonidine and dipivefrin, and the latter is no longer in clinical use. Brimonidine causes central nervous system (CNS) depression in infants and small children; if used in pregnancy, it should be discontinued closer to term and post-partum if breastfeeding.
Bimatoprost (prostaglandin analogue), timolol (beta blocker), and dorzolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) are all considered Category C according to the FDA classification system (Class C: drugs for which animal studies showed an adverse effect on the fetus, but there were no adequate studies in humans).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Glaucoma — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) has the best prognosis when a child is diagnosed at what age?
pool.rationale: The prognosis in PCG is best for children diagnosed between 3 and 12 months of age. The prognosis is worse when it is diagnosed within 1 month of life (newborn PCG) or at greater than 1 year of age. More than 50% of patients with newborn PCG develop legal blindness. The prognosis is also worse if the corneal diameters are larger than 14 mm at diagnosis.

pool.q: What artifact can be seen on visual field testing if a patient's head moves back from the machine during the test?
pool.rationale: It is important to assess for artifactual field loss when assessing visual field tests. If a lens is decentered, or a patient's head slides back from the forehead rest during the test, the lens rim can project into the central 30 degrees and cause a rim artifact. A cloverleaf pattern is generally seen when a patient loses attention and stops responding to stimuli after the early part of the test. A white scotoma is due to high false-positive errors that artifactually raise the threshold of the field. A lid artifact is due to ptosis.

pool.q: Once the aqueous humor leaves the anterior chamber, what is the order of intraocular structures through which it passes in the pressure-sensitive outflow pathway?

options.a: ciliary muscle, suprachoroidal space, scleral wall
options.b: ciliary muscle, Schlemm canal, outlet or collector channels, scleral wall
options.c: corneoscleral trabecular meshwork, juxtacanalicular meshwork, uveal trabecular meshwork, outlet or collector channels, Schlemm canal, episcleral veins
options.d: uveal trabecular meshwork, corneoscleral trabecular meshwork, juxtacanalicular meshwork, Schlemm canal, outlet or collector channels, episcleral veins

pool.rationale:
There are 2 major paths the aqueous takes to exit the eye that include the pressure-sensitive trabecular outflow and the pressure-insensitive uveoscleral outflow. To recall which is which, remember that "sensitive" and "trabecular" start with consonants and "insensitive" and "uveoscleral" start with vowels.
The pathway of aqueous through the pressure-sensitive trabecular outflow starts with the trabecular meshwork. The classically described layers of the trabecular meshwork are uveal (adjacent to anterior chamber, bands extending from the iris root/ciliary body to the peripheral cornea), corneoscleral (sheets of trabeculum from scleral spur to lateral wall of scleral sulcus), and juxtacanalicular (most outflow resistance, adjacent to/forms the inner wall of Schlemm canal). Of note, the trabecular cells are phagocytic, which is particularly relevant in the setting of inflammation and laser trabeculoplasty. (Mnemonic: Undercover job = uveal, corneoscleral, juxtacanalicular)
Next, the aqueous passes through Schlemm canal which resembles a lymphatic vessel. It is a single channel (200-300 μm) lined by an endothelial layer with a discontinuous basement membrane.
From Schlemm canal, approximately 25 to 30 collector channels arise and drain into the deep and midscleral venous plexi. Though not clearly delineated in the BCSC Glaucoma section, this is covered in the BCSC Fundamentals and Principles of Ophthalmology section.
Eventually, via a complex system of vessels, the aqueous reaches the episcleral veins and subsequently flows into the anterior ciliary and superior ophthalmic veins, which drain into the cavernous sinus.
The pressure-insensitive uveoscleral outflow likely has many paths; however, the answer choice "ciliary muscle, suprachoroidal space, scleral wall" describes the predominant one. The aqueous passes from the anterior chamber into the ciliary muscle, then into supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces and finally through intact sclera or along the nerves and vessels penetrating it. The uveoscleral pathway may account for up to 45% of total aqueous outflow. It is increased by cycloplegia, adrenergic agents, and prostaglandin analogues. It is decreased with age, glaucoma, and by miotics.
One of the remaining incorrect answers has the incorrect order, and the other is a mix of structures from the pressure-sensitive and pressure-insensitive pathways.

pool.q: A patient develops uncontrolled glaucoma several months after an extracapsular cataract extraction. A grayish, sheetlike opacity is noted on the superior corneal endothelial surface. What test will confirm the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Argon laser can confirm the diagnosis of epithelial ingrowth by producing white burns on the epithelial membrane and charcoal burns on normal iris surface. Extent of the ingrowth can also be demarcated by this method.
Anterior chamber paracentesis (tap) is not indicated; it can define an infectious reaction rather than an inflammatory reaction with rise in intraocular pressure.
Endothelial cell count may show a decreased cell number; however, specular microscopy would be a better diagnostic tool to define epithelial ingrowth, reversing the appearance of epithelial cells with dark centers and a lighter periphery.
Gonioscopy to reveal retained lens fragments in the angle would not be likely to produce a finding of epithelial downgrowth, although it may reveal an epithelial sheet in the angle. The majority of cases of glaucoma caused by epithelial downgrowth have normal gonioscopic findings.

pool.q: During the creation of a peripheral iridotomy, the 10 o'clock and 2 o'clock locations are avoided to decrease the risk of what complication?
pool.rationale:
Complications from iridotomy include bleeding, persistent postoperative inflammation, accelerated cataract formation, and lens damage. Retinal tear, postoperative IOP spike, and corneal endothelial damage can also occur.
Visual dysphotopsias (glare, streaks, lines, halos) may be present and are thought to result from proximity of the iridotomy to the tear meniscus, which acts as a strong prism. Thus, some clinicians advocate temporal placement of the iridotomy, taking precautions to perform the iridotomy at a distance from the tear meniscus. However, it is unclear whether the location of the iridotomy affects the likelihood of dysphotopsias, and a large prospective study suggests that it does not.

pool.q: What laser settings are best for performing a laser peripheral iridoplasty?

options.a: low power, short duration, small spot size
options.b: high power, short duration, small spot size
options.c: low power, long duration, large spot size
options.d: high power, long duration, large spot size

pool.rationale:
Laser iridoplasty is often used in plateau iris or other conditions with residual angle closure after an iridotomy. The goal is to create iris contraction peripherally, pulling the tissue from the angle. This requires a low and slow burn, using a large spot size. High powers ablate instead of shrink the tissue. Short durations do not allow enough time for adequate tissue shrinkage.

pool.q: A 44-year-old hyperopic Chinese woman is noted on slit-lamp examination to have shallow anterior chambers and clear lenses. Gonioscopy shows a convex iris profile with 360 degrees of iridotrabecular contact OU. On indentation gonioscopy, the scleral spur is visible for 360 degrees OU. Applanation IOP is 13 mm Hg OU and the optic nerves have healthy rims with a C:D ratio of 0.3 OU. What is the most likely mechanism of angle closure?
pool.rationale:
This patient has bilateral appositional angle closure without IOP elevation or optic nerve damage and can be categorized as a primary angle-closure suspect. Primary angle closure is multifactorial, and pupillary block is the most common mechanism. Pupillary block occurs when there is restricted movement through the pupil because of iris contact with the lens and is maximal when the pupil is in a mid-dilated position. The restricted flow of aqueous causes a pressure differential between the posterior and anterior chambers, resulting in forward bowing of the peripheral iris. The treatment for pupillary block angle closure is an iridotomy.
In plateau iris configuration, the anterior chamber is relatively deep, and the iris plane appears flat. Angle closure is caused by anteriorly positioned ciliary processes that push the peripheral iris forward.
Ciliary block is a rare form of secondary angle closure that usually presents following surgery in patients with primary angle closure. It presents with uniform shallowing or flattening of both the central and peripheral anterior chamber, with anterior displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm. In this patient with bilateral angle closure without any previous history of laser or surgery, ciliary block is extremely unlikely.
In phacomorphic angle closure, the predominant mechanism of angle closure is the mass effect of the lens. The lens is usually cataractous and causes a slow and progressive narrowing of the angle due to its bulk. In some cases, the onset may be rapid due to marked lens swelling (intumescent lens). In this patient with clear lenses, a phacomorphic mechanism is not likely to be the primary cause of angle closure.
